explanation: From T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant with gamma minus 1 = 2/3, the volume ratio is (T1 divided by T2) raised to the power 3/2, that is 4³⁄² = 8. Then from P V = n R T, the pressure ratio is (T2 divided by T1) times (V1 divided by V2) = (1/4) × (1/8) = 1/32.
The temperature drop is 300 K, so n R (T1 minus T2) = 1 × 8.3 × 300 = 2490 J. Dividing by gamma minus 1 = 0.4 gives 2490 divided by 0.4 = 6225 J.
For an isobaric process, W = PΔV = (1 × 10⁵)(0.004) = 400 J.
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, which remains constant in an isothermal process.
For a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas, PV^γ remains constant.
For an isobaric process, W = PΔV = (2 × 10⁵)(0.002) = 400 J.

correct_answer: Work and heat exchange are both zero
explanation: External pressure is zero and the container is insulated; thus Q = W = 0 and ΔU = 0.

correct_answer: From a colder body to a hotter body
explanation: Such reverse flow requires external work; spontaneous heat transfer is from hot to cold.

correct_answer: Heat flow through a finite temperature difference
explanation: A finite thermal gradient produces entropy and cannot be exactly reversed without additional changes.
Heat and work depend on the process path, whereas internal energy depends only on the thermodynamic state.

correct_answer: No heat is exchanged with the surroundings
explanation: Adiabatic means ΔQ = 0, although temperature, pressure and volume may change.

correct_answer: Can be reversed through infinitesimal changes without net effects
explanation: Reversibility requires quasistatic evolution without dissipative effects.
With no heat supplied, the gas does work at the expense of internal energy, so its temperature falls.
Quasistatic work is the integral ∫P dV, the signed area under the P–V curve.

correct_answer: The same temperature and no net heat flow
explanation: Temperature equality is the condition for thermal equilibrium.
Ideal-gas internal energy depends only on temperature, which remains constant.

correct_answer: Pressure changes more rapidly with volume in the adiabatic process
explanation: For an ideal gas, PV^γ is constant adiabatically while PV is constant isothermally; γ > 1 makes the adiabatic slope steeper.
Internal energy is a state function; the final state equals the initial state in a cycle.
At constant volume, dV = 0, so W = ∫P dV = 0.
It establishes transitive thermal equilibrium, allowing a thermometer to compare temperatures.

correct_answer: perfectly elastic, so that the total kinetic energy of the colliding molecules is conserved
explanation: Kinetic theory assumes that a gas molecule suffers no loss of kinetic energy in a collision. Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. This is why a gas kept at constant temperature in an insulated vessel maintains a steady pressure indefinitely; if any energy were lost per collision the pressure would keep decreasing.

correct_answer: a molecule spends almost all of its time in free straight line motion
explanation: If each collision lasts for a vanishingly small time, then almost the entire lifetime of a molecule is spent travelling freely in a straight line. This is what makes it meaningful to define a free path and a mean free path, and it also justifies calculating pressure as a sequence of instantaneous momentum transfers. The frequency of collisions can still be very large; a short duration does not mean a small number.

correct_answer: zero and a non zero positive quantity
explanation: Molecular motion is completely random, so for every molecule moving with a certain velocity there is on average another moving with the opposite velocity. The vector sum, and hence the average velocity, is zero for a container at rest. The square of a speed is always positive, so no cancellation is possible and the mean square speed is a definite positive number. That is exactly why pressure is written using the mean square speed and not the average velocity.

correct_answer: intermolecular forces are absent between collisions so that a molecule crosses the vessel at constant speed
explanation: The standard derivation follows one molecule bouncing between two opposite faces. Force free flight lets the transit time be written as twice the side length divided by the velocity component. Elastic collision at the wall makes the momentum change equal to twice the momentum component. Isotropy allows the mean square components along the three axes to be set equal, which produces the factor one third. A single common speed is never assumed; averaging over the distribution is what converts the sum of squared speeds into the mean square speed.

At low pressure the molecules are far apart, so their own volume is a negligible fraction of the vessel and the attractive forces are weak. At high temperature the average kinetic energy is large compared with the potential energy of attraction, so the attractive forces hardly affect the motion. Both requirements of the ideal gas model are therefore best satisfied at low pressure and high temperature.

correct_answer: along a straight line with constant velocity
explanation: Kinetic theory neglects intermolecular forces except during the brief collision. With zero net force the acceleration is zero, so the molecule travels in a straight line at constant speed. The straight segment between two collisions is exactly what is called a free path, and its average value is the mean free path.

correct_answer: the molecules occupy a finite volume and they attract one another
explanation: The ideal gas model assumes point molecules with no mutual force. A real molecule has a finite size, so the space available for motion is less than the vessel volume, which requires a volume correction. A real molecule also attracts its neighbours, so a molecule about to strike the wall is pulled back by the gas behind it and the measured pressure is smaller than the ideal value, which requires a pressure correction.

f = 2 × 20.75 / 8.3 = 41.5 / 8.3 = 5, so the molecule has five degrees of freedom and is a rigid diatomic. Then gamma = 1 + 2/5 = 1.40. Note that 20.75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is also the value of C_p for a monatomic gas, which is why the identification must be made from the definition and not from the number alone.
From gamma = 1 + 2/f we get gamma - 1 = 2/f, so f = 2 / (gamma - 1) = 2 / 0.5 = 4.

Heating one mole through one kelvin at constant volume requires C_v = (5/2) R of heat. Of the five degrees of freedom, three are translational, so the translational part of the energy rise is (3/2) R. The fraction is (3/2) R divided by (5/2) R = 3/5 = 0.6, the remaining 0.4 going into rotation.

At constant volume all the heat supplied raises the internal energy. At constant pressure the gas also does work R T per mole for a unit rise in temperature, so extra heat equal to R is needed per mole per kelvin. Hence C_p exceeds C_v by exactly R.

In thermal equilibrium the total energy of a molecule is shared equally among all its degrees of freedom, each receiving an average of (1/2) k T. Three translational modes therefore give 3 × (1/2) k T = (3/2) k T, which reproduces the standard translational result.
C_v = 1.5 × 8.3 = 12.45 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Then C_p = 12.45 + 8.3 = 20.75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, which is also (5/2) × 8.3.
With f = 5, C_v = (5/2) R and C_p = (7/2) R, so gamma = 7/5 = 1.40. Equivalently gamma = 1 + 2/5 = 1.40.
For the monatomic gas C_p = (3/2) R + R = (5/2) R. For the rigid diatomic gas C_p = (5/2) R + R = (7/2) R. The required ratio is (5/2) R divided by (7/2) R = 5/7.
A vibrating diatomic molecule has f = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Then C_v = (7/2) R, C_p = (9/2) R and gamma = 9/7 = 1.286, which is nearly 1.29.
Energy = 0.5 × 8.3 × 300 = 0.5 × 2490 = 1245 J. Multiplying by 3 gives 3735 J, the translational energy per mole, which confirms the arithmetic.
With f = 6, C_v = 3R and C_p = 4R, so gamma = 4R / 3R = 4/3 = 1.33. Equivalently gamma = 1 + 2/6 = 1.33.
A monatomic molecule has f = 3, so C_v = (3/2) R and C_p = C_v + R = (5/2) R. Therefore gamma = C_p / C_v = (5/2) / (3/2) = 5/3 = 1.67. The same follows from gamma = 1 + 2/3 = 1.67.

A diatomic molecule is a dumb bell. Its centre of mass can move along three independent directions, giving 3 translational modes. It can rotate about two axes perpendicular to the line joining the atoms, giving 2 rotational modes. Rotation about the bond axis itself has a negligible moment of inertia and is not counted, and the rigid model excludes vibration.

C_v of the mixture = (1 × 1.5R + 1 × 2.5R) / 2 = 4R / 2 = 2R, which is 16.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for R = 8.3. Then C_p = C_v + R = 3R and gamma = 3R / 2R = 1.5. The mixture behaves like a gas with four effective degrees of freedom.

A monatomic molecule is treated as a point mass, so its position needs three coordinates and its motion is fully described by three independent translational velocity components. Rotation of a point mass stores no energy and there are no interatomic bonds to vibrate, so the total is 3.

The translational kinetic energy of n moles is (3/2) n R T and involves neither the molar mass nor the atomicity. With n = 1 and the same T for both samples, the two energies are equal, so the ratio is 1 : 1. The atomicity would matter only if the total internal energy including rotation were asked for.

The expression contains only the Boltzmann constant, a universal number, and the absolute temperature. Pressure, volume, molar mass and the chemical identity of the gas are all absent. This is precisely why temperature can be interpreted as a direct measure of average molecular kinetic energy.

One mole contains N_A molecules and each has an average translational kinetic energy (3/2) k T. The total is N_A x (3/2) k T = (3/2) (N_A k) T = (3/2) R T, because the gas constant is the product of the Avogadro number and the Boltzmann constant.
Since the energy equals (3/2) k T, it is directly proportional to T. Doubling T doubles the energy. It is the root mean square speed that grows only as √(T), by a factor of 1.41 in this case.

correct_answer: the same for all three gases
explanation: The expression (3/2) k T contains only the Boltzmann constant and the absolute temperature. Neither the mass of the molecule nor the number of atoms in it appears. A heavier molecule compensates its larger mass with a smaller root mean square speed so that (1/2) m v_rms² stays the same.

correct_answer: the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules becomes zero
explanation: Because the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, it vanishes only when T = 0. Absolute zero is therefore the temperature at which the translational motion assumed by kinetic theory ceases, and it is why no lower temperature is possible on the Kelvin scale.

Each of the three translational degrees of freedom carries an average energy (1/2) k T by the law of equipartition. The total translational energy of one molecule is therefore 3 × (1/2) k T = (3/2) k T, and this value is the same for every ideal gas at a given temperature.
Translational energy per mole depends only on temperature, so both gases contribute (3/2) R T per mole. The total number of moles is 2 + 3 = 5. Energy = 1.5 × 5 × 8.3 × 300 = 1.5 × 12450 = 18675 J.

correct_answer: four times the initial energy and 1000 K
explanation: Since the energy varies as the square of the speed, doubling v_rms makes the energy 2² = 4 times its original value. Because the energy is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, the temperature must also become 4 times, that is 4 × 250 = 1000 K.
Energy per molecule = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ x 200 = 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J. Hence N = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁸ / 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ = 1000 molecules.
The initial absolute temperature is 27 + 273 = 300 K. To double the energy the absolute temperature must become 600 K. Converting back, 600 minus 273 = 327° celsius.
Reducing n to one fourth multiplies λ by 4. Halving d divides d² by 4 and therefore multiplies λ by another 4. The combined factor is 4 × 4 = 16.

The collision cross section is proportional to the square of the molecular diameter, and it appears in the denominator of λ = 1 / (√(2) π d² n). Doubling d multiplies d² by 4, so the mean free path falls to one fourth of its earlier value.

The mean free path is proportional to T and inversely proportional to P. The combined factor is (T_new / T_old) × (P_old / P_new) = 2 × (1/4) = 1/2. Hence the mean free path falls to half its initial value.

correct_answer: the average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions
explanation: Between two collisions a molecule travels a straight segment called a free path. These segments have different lengths, and their average value is the mean free path, usually written as λ. For air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure it is of the order of 10⁻⁷ m, far smaller than the size of any container.

At constant temperature the number density is proportional to the pressure, so doubling P doubles n. Since λ varies inversely as n, the mean free path falls to half. The same follows directly from λ = k T / (√(2) π d² P) with T fixed.

The more molecules there are in a given volume, the sooner a moving molecule meets one. In the standard expression λ = 1 / (√(2) π d² n), the number density appears in the denominator to the first power, so the mean free path is inversely proportional to n.

Density has dimensions M¹ L⁻³ and speed squared has dimensions L² T⁻². Their product is M¹ L⁻³ x L² T⁻² = M¹ L⁻¹ T⁻², which is exactly the dimensional formula of pressure. This confirms that P = (1/3) ρ v_rms² is dimensionally consistent, the numerical factor 1/3 being dimensionless.
Write P_new / P_old = (rho_new / rho_old) × (v_new / v_old)² = (1/2) × (3)² = (1/2) × 9 = 4.5. The pressure therefore becomes 4.5 times the initial value.

correct_answer: their molecules have the same root mean square speed
explanation: Rearranging the pressure expression gives v_rms = √(3P / ρ). If both P and ρ are the same for the two gases, then v_rms must be the same. Nothing follows about the molecular mass, since a gas of heavy molecules can reach the same density with fewer molecules per unit volume, and nothing follows about temperature because v_rms = √(3RT/M) involves the molar mass as well.

The density of the gas is the total mass N m divided by the volume V. Substituting ρ = N m / V into P = (1/3) ρ v_rms² gives P = (1/3) (N m / V) v_rms². The quantity N m / V has units kg m⁻³ and multiplying by the square of a speed gives Pa.

correct_answer: v_rms = √(3 R T / M), where M is the molar mass
explanation: For one mole the density is ρ = M / V. Substituting gives P = (1/3)(M / V) v_rms², that is P V = (1/3) M v_rms². Since P V = R T for one mole, R T = (1/3) M v_rms², so v_rms² = 3 R T / M and v_rms = √(3 R T / M). The molar mass must be taken in kilogram per mole for SI units.

Kinetic energy per unit volume is E = (1/2) ρ v_rms², so ρ v_rms² = 2E. Substituting in P = (1/3) ρ v_rms² gives P = (1/3) × 2E = (2/3) E. Equivalently the energy density is one and a half times the pressure.
From P = (1/3) ρ v_rms² we get v_rms² = 3P / ρ = 3 × 1.6 × 10⁵ / 3 = 1.6 × 10⁵. Taking the square root, v_rms = 400 m s⁻¹.

At constant density, P = (1/3) ρ v_rms² shows P proportional to v_rms². Doubling v_rms multiplies the pressure by 2² = 4. Physically each molecule now delivers twice the momentum per impact and strikes the wall twice as often, giving four times the force.

Since P = (2/3) E, the energy density is E = (3/2) P = 1.5 × 1.5 × 10⁵ = 2.25 × 10⁵ J m⁻³. Note that a joule per cubic metre and a pascal are the same combination of base units, so the answer is dimensionally consistent.

With the volume and molecular mass unchanged, the pressure is proportional to the product of the number of molecules and the square of the root mean square speed. The number falls to one half and the square of the speed rises by a factor of 2² = 4. Hence P_final / P = (1/2) × 4 = 2, so the final pressure is 2P.

Energy per unit volume is (3/2)P, so the total translational kinetic energy in a volume V is (3/2) P V = 1.5 × 2 × 10⁵ x 0.5 = 1.5 × 10⁵ J. The same result follows from (3/2) n R T combined with P V = n R T.

correct_answer: doubles, because the density doubles while v_rms stays the same
explanation: The root mean square speed depends only on temperature through v_rms = √(3RT/M), so an isothermal change leaves it unaltered. Halving the volume for a fixed mass doubles the density. Since P = (1/3) ρ v_rms² with v_rms fixed, the pressure doubles, which is exactly Boyle's law recovered from kinetic theory.

correct_answer: the mean square speed is shared equally among the three mutually perpendicular directions
explanation: For any molecule the squared speed is the sum of the squares of its three velocity components. Because the motion is random and isotropic, the averages of the three squared components are equal, so each equals one third of the mean square speed. Only the component perpendicular to a wall contributes to the momentum transfer at that wall, and this introduces the factor 1/3 into the pressure expression.

correct_answer: the root mean square speed is 4 times larger while the average kinetic energy is the same

correct_answer: a larger root mean square speed because v_rms varies inversely as the square root of molar mass
explanation: At the same temperature every molecule has the same average translational kinetic energy (3/2)kT. Since this equals (1/2) m v_rms², a smaller mass must be balanced by a larger speed. Numerically v_rms is proportional to 1 / √(M), and hydrogen with molar mass 2 g mol⁻¹ is far lighter than oxygen with 32 g mol⁻¹.

The molecular mass is unchanged, so v_rms is proportional to √(T). The temperature ratio is 800 / 200 = 4, giving a speed ratio of √(4) = 2. The new speed is 2 × 400 = 800 m s⁻¹. The value of the Boltzmann constant is not needed for a ratio question.
Setting 3 R T_oxygen / 32 = 3 R x 300 / 2 gives T_oxygen / 32 = 300 / 2 = 150, so T_oxygen = 150 × 32 = 4800 K. The heavier gas must be much hotter to match the speed of the lighter one.

correct_answer: the root mean square speed is unchanged and the total translational kinetic energy of the gas in the vessel is halved
explanation: The temperature is constant, so v_rms = √(3 R T / M) is unchanged. At constant volume and temperature the pressure is proportional to the number of molecules, so halving the pressure means half the molecules remain. The total translational kinetic energy is (3/2) N k T, which therefore falls to half. The same conclusion follows from (3/2) P V with V fixed and P halved.
To double the speed the absolute temperature must become 2² = 4 times, that is 4 × 300 = 1200 K. The required rise is 1200 minus 300 = 900 K.
Dividing the two expressions, v_rms / v_mp = √(3RT/M) / √(2RT/M) = √(3/2) = 1.2247, which is about 1.22. Equivalently the coefficients 1.73 and 1.41 give 1.73 / 1.41 = 1.22.
Since the root mean square speed corresponds to the coefficient 1.73, a value of 1730 m s⁻¹ means that √(R T / M) equals 1000 m s⁻¹. The mean speed then equals 1.60 × 1000 = 1600 m s⁻¹.
The ratio is √((T_A / M_A) / (T_B / M_B)) = √((2 T_B / 4 M_B) × (M_B / T_B)) = √(2 / 4) = √(1/2) = 1 / √(2), which is about 0.71. So gas A is the slower of the two despite being hotter.
Since v_rms = √(3 R T / M), the speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature. Multiplying T by 4 multiplies v_rms by √(4) = 2.

Writing each speed as a coefficient times √(R T / M), the coefficients are √(3) = 1.73 for the root mean square speed, √(8/π) = 1.60 for the mean speed and √(2) = 1.41 for the most probable speed. Hence v_rms is the largest and v_mp is the smallest.

correct_answer: zero and about 1.60 times √(R T / M)
explanation: Velocity is a vector, and in a stationary container every direction is equally likely, so the components cancel in pairs and the average velocity is zero. Speed is the magnitude of velocity and is always positive, so no cancellation is possible. The mean speed equals √(8 R T / π M), which is 1.60 times √(R T / M).
For one mole, P V = R T and P V = (1/3) M v_rms² from kinetic theory. Equating the two gives v_rms² = 3 R T / M, so v_rms = √(3 R T / M) with M in kilogram per mole.

The second overtone of an open pipe is the third harmonic, so the pipe holds three half wavelengths. Counting along the pipe there are antinodes at both ends and at two interior points, giving 4 antinodes, with 3 nodes in between.

correct_answer: the open pipe is twice as long as the closed pipe

The allowed frequencies are v/(2L), 2v/(2L), 3v/(2L) and so on. The first three are therefore in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.

The displacement antinode does not sit exactly at the geometric opening but a little beyond it, at a distance of about 0.3 times the inner diameter. A closed pipe has one open end and so needs one such correction, while an open pipe needs two.
The difference of the two resonance lengths is 0.74 - 0.24 = 0.50 m, which equals λ/2, so λ = 1 m. Hence f = v/λ = 330/1 = 330 Hz. This method automatically eliminates the end correction.
Consecutive odd harmonics differ by twice the fundamental, so 2 n = 700 - 500 = 200 Hz and n = 100 Hz. As a check, 500 = 5 × 100 and 700 = 7 × 100, which are indeed consecutive odd multiples.

correct_answer: the third harmonic, of frequency 3 n
explanation: The available frequencies are n, 3n, 5n and so on. The first frequency above the fundamental is 3n, so the first overtone is the third harmonic.

correct_answer: only the odd harmonics, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5

Frequencies below about 20 Hz are called infrasonic and are felt rather than heard, while frequencies above about 20000 Hz are ultrasonic and lie beyond the response of the human ear. The upper limit falls steadily with age, so the figure of 20 kHz applies to young ears.

correct_answer: the ground vibrations that travel ahead of an earthquake
explanation: Large slow moving masses produce very low frequencies. The ground motion associated with an earthquake contains components well below 20 Hz, which is why some animals appear to sense an earthquake before humans hear anything. Bats, SONAR transmitters and cleaning baths all operate above 20 kHz and are therefore ultrasonic sources.

correct_answer: The kinetic and potential energies keep changing but their sum stays constant
explanation: Adding (1/2) m omega² (A² - x²) and (1/2) m omega² x² gives (1/2) m omega² A², in which x does not appear. So energy is continually exchanged between the two forms while the total remains fixed.
E = 0.5 × 50 × 0.2² = 0.5 × 50 × 0.04 = 1 J. PE at x = 0.1 m is 0.5 × 50 × 0.01 = 0.25 J. Hence KE = 1 minus 0.25 = 0.75 J. The mass is not needed because the force constant is given.

The energy of an oscillating particle is proportional to the square of its amplitude, and the intensity of the wave is the energy crossing unit area per unit time. With the frequency and the medium unchanged, I is proportional to A². Tripling A therefore multiplies the intensity by 3² = 9.

Two successive compressions are the nearest pair of points that are in exactly the same state of motion and the same state of pressure. The distance between two such consecutive points in phase is by definition one wavelength. A compression and the rarefaction next to it are in opposite phase and are separated by half a wavelength.

correct_answer: light travels through air about a million times faster than sound, so the sound takes far longer to cover the same distance
explanation: The lightning and the thunder begin at the same moment. Light covers a few kilometres in a small fraction of a millisecond, so the flash is effectively seen at once. Sound covers the same few kilometres at about 340 m s⁻¹ and so takes several seconds. The gap therefore grows in proportion to the distance of the storm, which is why the delay is used to estimate that distance.

P is correct, since the air particles oscillate along the direction of travel. Q is wrong, because although energy travels forward each particle only oscillates about a fixed mean position and no net mass is carried across. R is correct, since a mechanical wave has nothing to propagate through in vacuum. S is wrong, because polarisation requires vibration across the line of travel and a longitudinal wave has none. Hence only P and R are correct.

correct_answer: a longitudinal mechanical wave in which the particles of air oscillate along the direction of propagation
explanation: In a sound wave the layers of air are alternately pushed together and pulled apart along the line of travel. Each particle oscillates about its mean position parallel to the direction in which the disturbance advances, which is the defining feature of a longitudinal wave. Because the restoring force comes from the elasticity of the air, the wave is mechanical, not electromagnetic.

correct_answer: energy travels from the speaker to the listener while each air particle merely oscillates about a fixed mean position
explanation: Each particle of air executes a small oscillation about its own mean position and hands its energy on to the next particle. Over one full cycle the net displacement of any particle is zero, so no air is carried across the room, yet the energy given out by the cone of the speaker travels outward continuously and reaches the ear.

correct_answer: becomes fainter and fainter and finally cannot be heard at all, although the hammer is still seen striking the gong
explanation: Sound is carried by the successive pushing of one layer of the medium on the next. As the air is removed there are fewer and fewer particles to pass the disturbance on, so the sound grows steadily fainter. In a good vacuum there is no medium at all and no sound reaches the jar wall, even though light still travels and the hammer is seen to move.

correct_answer: space contains no material medium, so the mechanical vibrations of sound have nothing to travel through, while radio waves need no medium
explanation: Sound propagates by the successive compression of layers of a material medium. Outer space is very nearly empty, so there are no layers of matter to be compressed and no sound can cross the gap. Radio waves are electromagnetic and propagate through vacuum without any medium, which is why they are used for communication in space.

correct_answer: the particles are crowded together, so that the density and the pressure are above their normal values
explanation: As the source vibrates it pushes the neighbouring layer of air forward, squeezing the particles into a smaller volume. In this region the number of particles per unit volume rises, so the density rises, and since the gas is compressed its pressure also rises above the undisturbed value. The opposite region, where the particles are pulled apart, is a rarefaction of reduced density and reduced pressure.

In every complete vibration the prong of the fork moves forward once, producing one compression, and backward once, producing one rarefaction. The fork completes 480 vibrations each second, so 480 compressions and 480 rarefactions leave it each second and 480 compressions cross any fixed point in the path in one second.

correct_answer: longitudinal waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases, while transverse mechanical waves can travel through the bulk of solids only
explanation: A longitudinal wave alternately compresses and expands the medium, and every state of matter resists a change of volume, so all three can carry it. A transverse wave requires the medium to resist a shearing displacement of one layer past another. Only solids possess a modulus of rigidity, so only solids can carry transverse mechanical waves through their bulk. Ripples on the surface of water are a surface effect governed by gravity and surface tension, not a bulk transverse wave.

The angular frequency is ω = 2 π f = 2 × 3.14 × 500 = 3140 rad s⁻¹. The amplitude is A = 1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m. Hence the maximum particle speed is A ω = 1 × 10⁻³ x 3140 = 3.14 m s⁻¹. This is roughly a hundred times smaller than the wave speed of 340 m s⁻¹, which confirms that the particles only jiggle while the disturbance races ahead.
Frequency counts oscillations per unit time. Since the oscillation count is a pure number, the unit is simply the reciprocal second, s⁻¹, given the special name hertz.

correct_answer: The period is independent of the amplitude of oscillation
explanation: The period expression involves only the inertia and the stiffness of the system. Increasing the amplitude increases both the distance to be covered and the restoring force in the same proportion, so the time taken per oscillation does not change. This property is called isochronism.
ω = 2 π f = 2 π x 50 = 100 π rad s⁻¹, which is about 314 rad s⁻¹.

correct_answer: 4 π rad s⁻¹, about 12.6 rad s⁻¹
explanation: f = 40/20 = 2 Hz, so the period is 0.5 s. Then ω = 2 π f = 2 π x 2 = 4 π rad s⁻¹, about 12.6 rad s⁻¹.

correct_answer: one quarter of its original value to make the period T/2
explanation: Since T is proportional to √(m), halving T requires √(m) to be halved, that is m must become one quarter of its original value. Checking, √(m/4) = (1/2) √(m).
From a = -100 x, omega² = 100 so ω = 10 rad s⁻¹. Then f = 10/(2 π) = 5/π Hz. In 60 s the number of oscillations is 60 × 5/π = 300/π, which is about 95.
Multiplying k by four divides T by √(4) = 2. The new period is therefore half the original period.

correct_answer: the resultant displacement at that point is the vector sum of the displacements produced by the individual waves
explanation: Because the wave equation is linear, if y1 and y2 are separately solutions then their sum is also a solution. Hence the net displacement of a particle is obtained by adding the individual displacements with their proper signs.

correct_answer: It follows from the linearity of the wave equation and applies to waves of every kind, including sound and light
explanation: If y1 and y2 each satisfy the linear wave equation, then any sum of them also satisfies it. Nothing in the argument refers to the type of wave, the direction of travel or the equality of frequencies.
The phase difference is (2 π/λ) × (λ/3) = 2 π/3. For two equal amplitudes, R = 2 A cos(φ/2) = 2 A cos(π/3) = 2 A x 0.5 = A.

correct_answer: the path difference between them is an integral multiple of the wavelength
explanation: Phase difference and path difference are related by phase = (2 π/λ) x path. For the phase difference to be 0, 2 π, 4 π and so on, the path difference must be 0, λ, 2 λ and so on.

The three phasors of equal length A are separated by 120°, so they form a closed equilateral triangle. Adding components, A cos 0 + A cos 120 + A cos 240 = A - 0.5 A - 0.5 A = 0, and A sin 0 + A sin 120 + A sin 240 = 0 as well. Hence the resultant amplitude is zero.

correct_answer: The wave velocity is constant for a given medium, while the particle velocity changes continuously during each oscillation
explanation: The wave velocity ω/k is fixed by the elastic and inertial properties of the medium and does not change with time. The particle velocity is the time derivative of the displacement and varies from zero at the extreme positions to A ω at the mean position.
Here A = 0.02 m, ω = 300 rad s⁻¹ and k = 1.5 rad m⁻¹. Maximum particle speed = 0.02 × 300 = 6 m s⁻¹ and wave speed = 300/1.5 = 200 m s⁻¹. The ratio is 6/200 = 0.03, which is also A k = 0.02 × 1.5.
A phase difference of π/2 rad corresponds to a path difference of λ/4. So λ/4 = 0.25 m, giving λ = 1 m. Then v = f λ = 500 × 1 = 500 m s⁻¹.
Comparison gives T = 0.02 s and λ = 40 cm = 0.4 m. Hence v = λ/T = 0.4/0.02 = 20 m s⁻¹.
Comparing with y = A sin(ω t - k x) gives ω = 200 π rad s⁻¹ and k = π rad m⁻¹. Hence v = ω/k = 200 π/π = 200 m s⁻¹. As a check, f = ω/2 π = 100 Hz and λ = 2 π/k = 2 m, so v = 100 × 2 = 200 m s⁻¹.
Keeping the phase constant, ω t - k x = constant, so x = (ω/k) t + constant. As time increases, x increases, so the wave advances along the positive x direction.

correct_answer: large compared with the wavelength of the sound and far enough away for the reflected sound to arrive after the direct sound has ceased to be sensed
explanation: Two conditions must be met. Geometrically, the reflector must be large compared with the wavelength, otherwise the sound bends around it. In time, the echo must arrive at least about 0.1 s after the direct sound, which for air at 340 m s⁻¹ places the reflector at least 17 m away. A hard dense surface reflects far better than a soft porous one.

correct_answer: a rarefaction, since a compression arriving at a free boundary is returned with the sign of the pressure change reversed
explanation: At the open end the air is free to move outward into the large body of atmosphere, so the excess pressure there must fall to the ambient value. The reflected pulse must therefore cancel the incident excess pressure at that point, which requires it to be a rarefaction. The displacement, in contrast, suffers no reversal at a free boundary. This is the exact opposite of what happens at a rigid wall.

The sound covers 165 m to the wall and 165 m back, a total of 330 m, in 1 s. Hence v = 330 / 1 = 330 m s⁻¹. This kind of open air measurement is the simplest classroom determination of the speed of sound.
The wavelength is λ = v / f = 1500 / 50000 = 0.03 m = 3 cm, short enough to give a well directed beam. The total path is v t = 1500 × 2 = 3000 m, so the depth is 3000 / 2 = 1500 m.

correct_answer: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane
explanation: Reflection is a general property of waves and does not depend on whether the wave is longitudinal or transverse. A sound wave striking a large rigid surface obeys exactly the same two laws as a light ray, and this is what makes sound reflectors, whispering galleries and megaphones work.
Path difference and phase difference are related by path = (λ/2 π) x phase. For a phase change of π this gives (0.6/2 π) x π = 0.3 m, that is half a wavelength.

correct_answer: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect
explanation: At a free end the boundary particle is unconstrained and is driven to twice the incident displacement, so it is an antinode and its displacement is certainly not zero. The uninverted reflection is exactly what makes this large displacement possible.
At a free boundary the end is able to move and in fact reaches maximum displacement. Incident and reflected displacements must add there rather than cancel, which requires zero phase change.

correct_answer: a phase change of π in the displacement but no phase change in the pressure variation
explanation: Zero net displacement at the wall requires the reflected displacement to be the negative of the incident displacement, a phase change of π. Pressure is related to the spatial gradient of displacement, so where displacement reverses the pressure does not, and the pressure variations add at the wall.

correct_answer: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode
explanation: At the open end the air is free to expand into the atmosphere, so the excess pressure there must stay close to zero. The reflected pressure wave is therefore inverted, and a compression returns as a rarefaction, while the displacement is unreversed and maximum, making the end an antinode.

correct_answer: only the direction of propagation and, at a rigid boundary, the phase
explanation: The source continues to vibrate at the same rate, so the frequency of the reflected wave equals that of the incident wave. The medium is the same, so the speed is the same, and therefore λ = v/f is also the same. Only the direction reverses, together with a phase change of π if the boundary is rigid.

correct_answer: The reflected pulse is inverted, because the heavier string behaves as the denser and more rigid medium
explanation: The wave speed on a string is √(T/m), so a heavier string carries the wave more slowly and acts as the denser medium. Reflection from a denser medium introduces a phase change of π, which appears as an inverted reflected pulse, while the pulse transmitted into the heavy string stays erect.
The two terms have the same angular frequency π rad s⁻¹ but differ in phase by π/2, so they combine like perpendicular vectors. The resultant amplitude is √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √(25) = 5 cm.

correct_answer: Velocity leads displacement by π/2 rad and acceleration leads velocity by π/2 rad
explanation: Each differentiation with respect to time advances the phase of a sinusoid by π/2. Hence velocity is ahead of displacement by π/2 and acceleration is ahead of velocity by a further π/2, making it π ahead of displacement.
If x = A sin(ω t), then v = A ω sin(ω t + π/2) and a = A omega² sin(ω t + π). Subtracting the phase of v from the phase of a gives π minus π/2, which is π/2 rad.

From the two conditions, 16 = omega² (A² - 9) and 9 = omega² (A² - 16). Subtracting gives 7 = omega² x 7, so ω = 1 rad s⁻¹. Substituting back gives A² = 25, that is A = 5 cm. Hence T = 2 π / 1 = 2 π s, about 6.28 s.
At the mean position x = 0, so v = ω √(A² - 0) = ω A. This is the largest speed reached during the oscillation.

correct_answer: the net force on it is proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed opposite to that displacement
explanation: SHM is defined by F = -k x with k positive. This single condition guarantees a = -omega² x, sinusoidal displacement, and a period independent of amplitude.

correct_answer: oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic
explanation: The acceleration is directed towards x = 0 because of the negative sign, so the particle oscillates about x = 0. However SHM demands a = -omega² x, a first power relation. Here a varies as the cube of x, so the motion is oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic.

correct_answer: directly proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it
explanation: Dividing F = -k x by the mass m gives a = -(k/m) x = -omega² x. So the magnitude of acceleration grows in direct proportion to x, and its sign is always opposite to that of x.

correct_answer: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on any diameter of the reference circle
explanation: If a reference particle moves on a circle of radius A with constant angular speed ω, its position vector makes an angle ω t + φ with a chosen axis. The foot of the perpendicular from this particle to any diameter has displacement A cos(ω t + φ), which is exactly linear SHM of amplitude A.
From F = -k x, the magnitude of k is force divided by displacement. Force is measured in N and displacement in m, so k is measured in N per m, written N m⁻¹.
Here k = 8 N m⁻¹ and m = 2 kg, so omega² = k/m = 8/2 = 4 and ω = 2 rad s⁻¹. Then T = 2 π / ω = 2 π / 2 = π s, which is about 3.14 s.

correct_answer: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
explanation: Putting x = 0 gives v = ω √(A²) = A ω, the largest possible speed, and a = -omega² x = 0.
Magnitude of F = k x = 200 × 0.05 = 10 N. The direction is towards the mean position.
L2/L1 = 1.21, so T2/T1 = √(1.21) = 1.1. Hence T2 = 1.1 × 2 = 2.2 s, an increase of 10% in the period for a 21% increase in length.
g_eff = 10 + 10 = 20 m s⁻². Hence T2 = T1 √(g/g_eff) = 2 x √(10/20) = 2 divided by √(2) = √(2) s, which is about 1.41 s.
A second pendulum has a period of 2 s, so f = 1/T = 1/2 = 0.5 Hz. It completes half an oscillation every second.
Since T is proportional to √(L), multiplying L by four multiplies T by √(4) = 2. The period therefore doubles.

correct_answer: only for small angles can sin(θ) be replaced by θ, which makes the restoring force proportional to the displacement
explanation: The tangential restoring force on the bob is m g sin(θ). SHM requires a force proportional to the displacement, which is satisfied only when sin(θ) can be replaced by θ, that is for small θ expressed in radian. For larger amplitudes the true period is slightly greater than 2 π √(L/g).
A second pendulum is defined so that each one way swing takes exactly 1 s. Since one complete oscillation contains two such swings, the period is 2 s and the frequency is 0.5 Hz.

correct_answer: decreases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g + a
explanation: In the frame of the accelerating lift a pseudo force acts downward on the bob, so the effective acceleration due to gravity is g + a. Since T is inversely proportional to √(g_eff), a larger g_eff gives a shorter period.
A decrease of 2% in g gives dg/g = -0.02. Then dT/T = -(1/2)(-0.02) = +0.01, an increase of 1%. Hence T = 2 × 1.01 = 2.02 s, and the pendulum clock would run slow.

correct_answer: equal, because the period does not depend on the mass of the bob
explanation: The restoring force is m g sin(θ) and the inertia is m, so the acceleration g sin(θ) is independent of m. The period expression therefore contains only L and g, and the two pendulums have equal periods.

correct_answer: a curve that rises with decreasing steepness, while the graph of v against √(T) is a straight line through the origin
explanation: Writing the Laplace formula with the gas relation gives v = √(gamma R T / M), so v is proportional to the square root of T. A square root curve rises steeply at first and then flattens, so v against T bends over. If instead √(T) is plotted along the horizontal axis the relation becomes linear and the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is √(gamma R / M).

Since gamma is the same for both, equal speeds require T_X / M_X = T_Y / M_Y. With M_Y = 4 M_X this gives T_Y = 4 T_X = 4 × 300 = 1200 K. Physically, the heavier gas is four times as sluggish in molar mass, so its absolute temperature must be four times as high to give its molecules the same characteristic speed and hence the same speed of sound.

correct_answer: greater, because water vapour is less dense than the air it displaces
explanation: Water vapour has a molar mass of 18 g, while nitrogen has 28 g and oxygen has 32 g. When water vapour is added at fixed total pressure and temperature it displaces some of these heavier molecules, so the density of the mixture falls. Since v = √(gamma P / ρ), a smaller ρ gives a larger speed, and sound therefore travels faster on a humid day.

correct_answer: remains unchanged, because the density doubles along with the pressure so that P / ρ is unaltered
explanation: Doubling the pressure of a gas at constant temperature packs the same molecules into half the volume, so the density also doubles. In v = √(gamma P / ρ) the numerator and the denominator change by the same factor, leaving the ratio and hence the speed unchanged. This is confirmed by the ideal gas relation P / ρ = R T / M, which shows that P / ρ depends only on temperature for a given gas.

Writing P / ρ = R T / M turns the Laplace formula into v = √(gamma R T / M). With gamma and T the same for both gases, v is proportional to 1 / √(M). Hence v_H / v_O = √(M_O / M_H) = √(32 / 2) = √(16) = 4. Sound travels four times faster in hydrogen than in oxygen at the same temperature.

correct_answer: isothermally, so that the temperature of the gas stays constant throughout the passage of the wave
explanation: Newton argued that the heat produced in a compression would have time to flow into the neighbouring rarefaction, keeping the temperature uniform. For an isothermal change of an ideal gas the bulk modulus equals the pressure P, so his formula became v = √(P / ρ). Numerically this gives about 280 m s⁻¹ for air, some fifteen per cent below the measured value.
With gamma and P the same for the two gases, v varies as 1 / √(ρ). If rho_1 = 4 rho_2 then v₁ / v₂ = √(rho_2 / rho_1) = √(1/4) = 1/2. The denser gas therefore carries sound at half the speed.
Y / ρ = 2 × 10¹¹ / 8 × 10³ = 2.5 × 10⁷ m² s⁻². Taking the square root gives v = 5 × 10³ = 5000 m s⁻¹. Sound therefore travels through steel about fifteen times faster than through air.

correct_answer: the same for all audible frequencies, which is why a distant band is heard in tune and in time
explanation: The speed of sound follows entirely from the elastic and inertial properties of the medium. Neither the frequency nor the amplitude of the disturbance appears in the expression. Hence all audible frequencies travel through the same air at the same speed, which is why a chord played at a distance still sounds as a chord.
1/k_eq = 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so k_eq = 2 N m⁻¹. Note that the series value is smaller than either individual constant, as it must be.

Springs in parallel undergo the same extension x. The total restoring force is k1 x + k2 x = (k1 + k2) x, so the equivalent force constant is k1 + k2. A parallel combination is always stiffer than either spring alone.
T_series = 2 π √(m/(k/2)) = 2 π √(2 m/k) and T_parallel = 2 π √(m/(2 k)). Their ratio is √(2 m/k) divided by √(m/(2 k)) = √(4) = 2, that is 2 : 1.
Cutting the spring in half doubles its force constant to 2 k. Since T is inversely proportional to √(k), the new period is T divided by √(2) = 2 divided by 1.414 = √(2) s, about 1.41 s.
Since λ/2 = 20 cm, λ = 40 cm = 0.4 m. Then v = f λ = 250 × 0.4 = 100 m s⁻¹.
With x = λ/12, k x = (2 π/λ)(λ/12) = π/6. The amplitude is 2 A sin(π/6) = 2 A x 0.5 = A, while the antinode amplitude is 2 A. The ratio is A : 2 A, that is 1 : 2.
The space factor of a stationary wave is sin(k x), which vanishes whenever k x is a multiple of π. Successive zeros are separated by π/k = λ/2.
Here k = π/6 rad m⁻¹, so λ = 2 π/k = 12 m, and ω = 20 π rad s⁻¹, so f = 10 Hz. Hence v = f λ = 10 × 12 = 120 m s⁻¹, which is also ω/k = 20 π/(π/6).

correct_answer: In a progressive wave every particle has the same amplitude, while in a stationary wave the amplitude varies with position from zero to a maximum
explanation: In the progressive form the coefficient of the oscillating factor is the constant A. In the stationary form the coefficient is 2 A sin(k x), which depends on where the particle is, giving zero at nodes and 2 A at antinodes.
The whole pattern becomes flat when cos(ω t) = 0, which happens at t = T/4 and t = 3T/4 in each period, that is twice in every period.
Since sin(k x) is positive in one loop and negative in the next, the displacements of particles in adjacent loops always have opposite signs, which corresponds to a phase difference of π.

correct_answer: π/2 m, that is about 1.57 m
explanation: Adding the two waves gives y = 10 sin(2 x) cos(4 t) apart from sign conventions. The nodes are where sin(2 x) = 0, that is 2 x = 0, π, 2 π and so on, so consecutive nodes are π/2 m apart. Equivalently λ = 2 π/2 = π m and λ/2 = π/2 m.
Here k = π/3 rad m⁻¹, so λ = 2 π/k = 6 m. Consecutive nodes are separated by λ/2 = 3 m. Directly, sin(π x/3) vanishes at x = 0, 3, 6 metre and so on.

correct_answer: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(ω t)
explanation: Adding y1 = A sin(ω t - k x) and y2 = A sin(ω t + k x) gives y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(ω t) after using the sum to product identity. The position fixes the amplitude and the time factor is shared by all particles.
With x = λ/8, k x = (2 π/λ)(λ/8) = π/4. Hence the amplitude is 2 A sin(π/4) = 2 A/√(2) = A √(2), about 1.41 A.

correct_answer: has zero amplitude and stays permanently at rest
explanation: The amplitude factor 2 A sin(k x) vanishes at the nodes for every value of time, so a particle located there never moves.
Three loops in 1.5 m means each loop is 0.5 m, so λ = 1 m. The wave speed is v = f λ = 100 × 1 = 100 m s⁻¹. Hence T = m v² = 0.02 × 100² = 0.02 × 10000 = 200 N.

correct_answer: two nodes at the ends and one antinode at the middle, with L = λ/2
explanation: Both ends are held fixed and must be nodes. The simplest pattern satisfying this has a single loop with one antinode in the middle, and one loop spans half a wavelength, so L = λ/2.
The tension and linear density are common to all three segments, so n is proportional to 1/L. The reciprocals of 1, 2 and 3 are 1, 1/2 and 1/3, which on multiplying throughout by 6 become 6 : 3 : 2.
The ratio of tensions is 225/100 = 2.25, whose square root is 1.5. Hence n2 = 200 × 1.5 = 300 Hz.
The fundamental wavelength is 2L = 2 m, so v = f λ = 100 × 2 = 200 m s⁻¹. Since v = √(T/m), T = m v² = 0.01 × 200² = 0.01 × 40000 = 400 N.
For the expression √(T/m) to have the unit of speed, T in N divided by m must give m² s⁻². Since N is kg m s⁻², m must be in kg m⁻¹, which is indeed mass per unit length.

correct_answer: inversely proportional to the vibrating length
explanation: Since n = (1/2L) √(T/m), keeping T and m fixed makes n proportional to 1/L, so the product n L stays constant.
In the fundamental mode the string carries one loop, so L = λ/2 and λ = 2L. Since v = √(T/m), the frequency is n = v/λ = (1/2L) √(T/m).
The wave speed is v = √(100/0.01) = √(10000) = 100 m s⁻¹. The fundamental frequency is n = v/(2L) = 100/(2 × 0.5) = 100 Hz.
Each loop is 1.2/4 = 0.3 m long and equals λ/2, so λ = 0.6 m. Hence v = f λ = 200 × 0.6 = 120 m s⁻¹.
Comparison with the standard form shows T = 0.01 s and λ = 3.4 m. Hence the frequency is f = 1 / T = 100 Hz and the speed is v = f λ = 100 × 3.4 = 340 m s⁻¹, the usual speed of sound in air.
T = 1 / f = 1 / 2000 s = 5 × 10⁻⁴ s = 0.5 ms. Each complete vibration of the source therefore takes half a millisecond.
λ = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m. The note therefore repeats itself in space every 68 cm as it travels through the air.

The frequency is the same in both media because it is fixed by the source. Hence λ is proportional to v and lambda_air / lambda_water = 340 / 1500. Dividing both numbers by 20 gives 17 / 75. The wavelength in water is therefore several times longer than in air.

The particles at the boundary are driven by the wave arriving from the air, so they vibrate at exactly the rate at which the source vibrates. That rate is carried unchanged into the water. The speed, however, is fixed by the elasticity and density of the new medium and is much larger in water. Since λ = v / f with f fixed and v larger, the wavelength in water is correspondingly larger.
One complete cycle of 360° corresponds to a path difference of one wavelength. A phase difference of 60° is therefore 60 / 360 = 1 / 6 of a cycle, so the separation is λ / 6.
Using φ = (2 π / λ) x delta x with delta x = λ / 4 gives φ = (2 π / λ) × (λ / 4) = π / 2 rad, which is 90° or a quarter of a cycle.

correct_answer: the distance travelled by the wave in the time taken by one particle of the medium to complete one full oscillation
explanation: In the time T taken by a particle to complete one oscillation, the disturbance advances by a distance v T. After that time the pattern has moved forward by exactly one repeat unit, so v T is the wavelength. Writing T = 1/f gives the standard relation v = f λ.

Doubling the separation halves the capacitance. With the charge fixed, U = Q² / (2 C) doubles. The extra energy is supplied by the external agent that pulls the oppositely charged plates apart against their attraction.
The effective separation is d - t + t / K = 5 - 3 + 3 / 3 = 5 - 3 + 1 = 3 mm. So C changes from ε₀ A / 5 mm to ε₀ A / 3 mm, a factor of 5 / 3.

correct_answer: its geometry and the medium filling the space between its conductors
explanation: Increasing the charge on a capacitor raises its potential difference in exact proportion, so the ratio Q / V is unchanged. What does change the capacitance is the plate area, the separation, the shape of the conductors and the dielectric constant of the medium between them.
C = 2 × 10⁻⁴ / 20 = 1 × 10⁻⁵ F, that is 10 microF. At 50 V the charge is Q = 1 × 10⁻⁵ x 50 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ C, which is 2.5 times the original charge, matching the ratio 50 to 20.

correct_answer: the capacitance and the stored charge both rise K times while the field between the plates is unchanged
explanation: The battery holds the potential difference V constant. The capacitance becomes K C₀, so the charge Q = C V becomes K times larger, drawn from the battery. The field between the plates is E = V / d, and since neither V nor d changes, the field is unchanged.

Capacitance is the charge stored per unit rise of potential, C = Q / V, so the unit is coulomb per volt. This unit is named the farad. One farad is a very large capacitance, so practical capacitors are rated in microfarad or picofarad.
Capacitance is inversely proportional to the plate separation, so doubling the separation halves it. The new value is 12 / 2 = 6 microF.

The equivalent capacitance is 2 × 3 / (2 + 3) = 1.2 microF, so the common charge is Q = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ x 100 = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ C. Then the potential difference across the 2 microF capacitor is 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ / (2 × 10⁻⁶) = 60 V and across the 3 microF capacitor it is 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ / (3 × 10⁻⁶) = 40 V. These add to 100 V, as they must.

correct_answer: the charge is the same on each capacitor in a series arrangement, while the potential difference is the same across each in a parallel arrangement
explanation: In a series chain the inner plates are isolated, so induction gives every capacitor the same charge while the applied voltage divides between them. In a parallel arrangement all the capacitors are connected across the same two nodes, so they share the same potential difference while the charge divides in proportion to the capacitances.
For n identical capacitors of value C, the parallel equivalent is n C and the series equivalent is C / n. Their ratio is n², which is 16 for n = 4.

Let the initial energy be U. With the battery connected the voltage is fixed and the capacitance doubles, so the energy becomes 2 U, the extra energy coming from the battery. With the battery disconnected the charge is fixed and the capacitance doubles, so the energy becomes U / 2, the difference being spent in drawing the slab in. The ratio is 2 U to U / 2, that is 4 : 1.

The parallel pair gives 6 + 6 = 12 microF. Combining this in series with 6 microF gives 1 / C = 1 / 12 + 1 / 6 = 1 / 12 + 2 / 12 = 3 / 12, so C = 4 microF, which is less than the smallest capacitance in the series part of the network.
1 / C = 1 / 3 + 1 / 6 = 2 / 6 + 1 / 6 = 3 / 6 = 1 / 2, so C = 2 microF, which is smaller than either capacitor.

In the metal the free electrons keep moving until the induced surface charges create a field that exactly cancels the applied field, so the internal field is zero. In the dielectric the charges are bound and can only be displaced slightly, so the bound surface charges produce a partial opposing field and the net field is reduced to E / K, here E / 4. A conductor can be regarded as the limiting case of a dielectric with an infinitely large dielectric constant.

correct_answer: entirely on the outer surface of the sphere
explanation: If any excess charge remained inside the metal, it would produce a field there and drive further motion, contradicting equilibrium. The mutual repulsion of like charges also pushes them as far apart as possible. Both arguments lead to the same conclusion: the excess charge sits entirely on the outer surface.

correct_answer: molecules of a polar dielectric have a permanent dipole moment even with no field applied
explanation: In a non polar molecule such as hydrogen the centres of positive and negative charge coincide, so the molecule has no dipole moment until a field pulls the centres apart. In a polar molecule such as water the two centres are permanently separated, so a dipole moment exists even with no field. In the absence of a field these permanent dipoles point randomly, so the material shows no net polarisation until a field aligns them.

Charges induced on the outside of the metal enclosure arrange themselves so that the field inside the cavity is zero, whatever the external field. The interior is therefore protected, and this protection is called electrostatic shielding. The same principle keeps a person safe inside a car during a lightning strike.

correct_answer: acquire or align dipole moments, producing bound charges on the faces of the slab
explanation: The applied field displaces the positive and negative charges within each molecule slightly, or aligns dipoles that are already present. Inside the slab the effects of neighbouring molecules cancel, but bound charges are left uncancelled on the two faces. These bound charges set up a field opposing the applied field, so the net field inside the dielectric is reduced.

correct_answer: a dimensionless number that is greater than or equal to 1
explanation: K is the ratio of two quantities of the same kind, so it carries no unit and no dimensions. Because polarisation always weakens the field inside the dielectric, the reduced field is smaller than the applied one and K is at least 1, equalling 1 only for vacuum.
E_inside = E_applied / K = 3 × 10⁴ / 3 = 1 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. The field set up by the bound surface charges is the difference, 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹, directed against the applied field.

Free electrons in the metal move under the applied field and pile up on the surfaces. Their own field opposes the applied field, and the movement continues until the two cancel exactly. Once that happens no force acts on the remaining free charges, so equilibrium is reached with zero field everywhere inside the conductor.

correct_answer: negative charge on its left face and equal positive charge on its right face
explanation: The field pushes positive charge to the right, but only electrons are free to move, and they move to the left, against the field. The left face therefore acquires negative charge and the right face is left with an equal positive charge. These induced charges produce an internal field to the left that exactly cancels the applied field inside the metal.

correct_answer: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time, each force being unaffected by the presence of the remaining charges
explanation: Coulomb's law describes a two body interaction. The force between any pair of charges is exactly the same whether or not other charges are present, and the resultant is obtained by vector addition of these pairwise forces.
ε₀ has dimensions of (A T)² divided by (M L T⁻²)(L²), that is A² T² / (M L³ T⁻²) = M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A².

After the third sphere touches X, both carry (5 + 0) / 2 = 2.5 microC. The third sphere, now at 2.5 microC, touches Y, and the two share (2.5 - 3) / 2 = -0.25 microC each. F' = F / K = 8 / 80 = 0.1 N. Water polarises strongly, so it reduces the electrostatic force to one eightieth of its value in air.

In a medium the permittivity becomes epsilon = K ε₀, so F = q1 q2 / (4 π K ε₀ r²) = F_vacuum / K. With K = 5 the force falls to F / 5.

correct_answer: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the separation
explanation: Coulomb's law states F = k q1 q2 / r². The numerator carries the product of the two charges and the denominator the square of the distance between them, so the force falls to one quarter when the separation is doubled.

correct_answer: their separation is very large compared with their radii
explanation: When the spheres are close together each sphere induces a redistribution of charge on the other, so the charge is no longer uniformly distributed and the centres are no longer the effective locations of the charge. Only when the separation is much larger than the radii can each sphere be treated as a point charge at its centre.
F2 = F1 × (r1 / r2)² = 16 × (1/2)² = 16 / 4 = 4 N. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter of its original value.
With ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the combination 1 / (4 π ε₀) works out to about 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². This is the standard value of k used in numerical problems.
In a medium the permittivity becomes epsilon = K ε₀, so the force is F' = q1 q2 / (4 π K ε₀ r²) = F / K. For water with K about 80 the force falls to one eightieth of its vacuum value.

correct_answer: both vary as the inverse square of distance, but only the Coulomb force can be repulsive and depends on the medium
explanation: Both forces act along the line joining the two bodies and both fall off as 1 / r². The differences are that charge comes in two signs so the Coulomb force can attract or repel while gravitation only attracts, that the Coulomb force is reduced by a factor K in a dielectric while gravitation is unaffected by the intervening medium, and that the Coulomb force is about 10³⁶ times stronger for two protons.
q² = F r² / k = 0.9 × 1 / (9 × 10⁹) = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ C². Taking the square root gives q = 1 × 10⁻⁵ C, that is 10 microC on each sphere.

Consider one of the end charges. The other end charge repels it with k q² / r² outward. The midpoint charge Q is at distance r / 2 and must attract it inward with k q |Q| / (r/2)² = 4 k q |Q| / r². Equating gives |Q| = q / 4, and the charge must be negative, so it is -q / 4. The midpoint charge is itself in equilibrium by symmetry.

F = k q (Q - q) / r². Writing the product as q Q - q² and setting the derivative with respect to q to zero gives Q - 2 q = 0, so q = Q / 2. Equivalently, the product of two numbers with a fixed sum is largest when they are equal.
F' = k (2 q1)(2 q2) / (2 r)² = 4 k q1 q2 / (4 r²) = k q1 q2 / r² = F. The two effects cancel exactly.

Both forces vary as the inverse square of the separation, so the distance cancels in the ratio. Substituting k = 9 × 10⁹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ and m_p = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg gives a ratio of about 10³⁶. Electrostatic forces are therefore overwhelmingly dominant at the level of individual particles.

correct_answer: the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
explanation: Coulomb's law gives the same expression k q1 q2 / r² for the force on each charge, because the same product of charges and the same separation appear. The forces act along the line joining the charges and point in opposite senses, forming a Newton third law pair, even though the charges and the masses may be very different.
Equating the two forces gives 1 / r² = 1 / (K r'²), so r'² = r² / K and r' = r / √K = 20 / 2 = 10 cm.
Tripling one charge multiplies the numerator by 3. Halving the separation divides the denominator by 4, which multiplies the force by 4. The overall factor is 3 × 4 = 12, so the new force is 12 F.
Total charge = (+3) + (-5) + (+7) microC = +5 microC. Charge is a scalar and adds algebraically, so signs must be carried through the sum.

correct_answer: X carries +1 microC and Y carries -1 microC
explanation: Charge transferred = n e = 6.25 × 10¹² x 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ C = 1 microC. X has lost these electrons, so X is left with +1 microC, and Y which received them carries -1 microC. The algebraic total is still zero.

correct_answer: both leaves receive charge of the same sign and repel each other
explanation: Charge given to the disc spreads over the whole conductor, so each leaf gets charge of the same sign. Like charges repel, so the leaves swing apart. The angle of divergence is a rough measure of the charge given.
Charge exists only in packets of size e. Writing q = n e with n a positive or negative integer expresses exactly this, and the property is named quantisation of charge.

The negative rod repels free electrons to the far side of the sphere. Earthing lets those electrons flow away to the ground. Breaking the earth connection first traps a deficiency of electrons, so when the rod is removed the sphere is left positively charged, opposite in sign to the rod.
Rubbing only transfers electrons from one body to the other. If a charge -q appears on one body then +q appears on the other, so the algebraic total remains zero, the value it had before rubbing.
q = n e = 10¹² x 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ C. Because electrons have been removed, the ball is left with a deficiency of negative charge and so carries +1.6 × 10⁻⁷ C.

correct_answer: P is true and Q is false
explanation: Charge conservation says the algebraic total charge of an isolated system never changes, so P is true. Charge is also invariant, meaning a given particle carries the same charge whether it is at rest or moving fast, so Q is false. Mass, unlike charge, does depend on speed at relativistic speeds.

Number of electrons gained n = (1.6 × 10⁻⁷) / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 10¹². Mass gained = 10¹² x 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ = 9.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg. Since the rod becomes negative it has gained electrons, so its mass increases by this utterly negligible amount.

correct_answer: negative charge on the near face, positive charge on the far face and zero net charge
explanation: Free electrons in the metal are drawn towards the positive rod, so the near face acquires negative charge and the far face is left positive. Since the sphere is isolated, no charge enters or leaves it and its net charge stays zero.
Because charge exists only in packets of size e, the change in charge on transferring n electrons is n e. The smallest non zero value corresponds to n = 1, that is a change of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

R is uncharged at the start of every contact because it is discharged each time. So each contact shares the charge on P equally and halves it. After the first contact P holds Q/2, after the second Q/4, and after the third Q/8.

correct_answer: electrons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth
explanation: Only the loosely bound electrons can be transferred by rubbing. The glass rod ends up positive, so it must have lost electrons, that is electrons went from the glass to the silk. The silk becomes equally negative.

correct_answer: the elementary charge is so small that ordinary charges correspond to enormous values of n
explanation: A charge of only 1 microC already corresponds to n = 10⁻⁶ / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹), which is about 6.25 × 10¹². Adding or removing one electron changes such a charge by a fraction of order 10⁻¹³, far below any measurable resolution, so the charge appears to vary continuously.

correct_answer: 0°, and this position is one of stable equilibrium

correct_answer: from the negative charge towards the positive charge

correct_answer: zero net force and a non zero torque
explanation: In a uniform field the forces q E and -q E on the two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel and the net force is zero. Their lines of action are different, so they constitute a couple of moment p E sin θ, which is non zero unless the dipole is aligned or antialigned with the field.

The two charges sit at slightly different values of x, where the field magnitudes differ. The net force is p times the rate of change of E with x. Here that rate is 1000 N C⁻¹ per metre, so F = 1 × 10⁻⁶ x 1000 = 1 × 10⁻³ N, directed towards the region of stronger field.
The maximum torque equals p E, so p E = 4 N m. Turning the dipole from θ = 0 to θ = 180° requires W = p E (cos 0 - cos 180) = p E (1 + 1) = 2 p E = 8 J.

At 90° the potential energy is -p E cos 90 = 0 and at 0° it is -p E. The energy released is therefore p E, all of which appears as rotational kinetic energy at the aligned position: (1/2) I omega² = p E, so ω = √(2 p E / I).
p = 2 × 10⁻⁶ x 0.05 = 1 × 10⁻⁷ C m, directed from the negative charge to the positive charge.
The torque magnitude p E sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1, that is at θ = 90°, where the dipole axis is perpendicular to the field.
p E = 1 × 10⁻⁶ x 1 × 10⁵ = 0.1 J. Starting at θ = 0 and ending at θ = 60°, W = p E (cos 0 - cos 60) = 0.1 × (1 - 0.5) = 0.05 J.

correct_answer: Two field lines can never cross each other
explanation: If two field lines crossed, the field at the point of crossing would have two different directions at once, which is impossible. Electrostatic lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, are never closed, and do not pass through conductors.

correct_answer: adding the individual fields as vectors
explanation: Each charge sets up its own field at the point as though the others were absent, and the resultant field is the vector sum of these contributions. Because the field is a vector, both magnitude and direction of every contribution must be taken into account.
E2 = E1 × (r1 / r2)² = 400 × (1/2)² = 400 / 4 = 100 N C⁻¹. Doubling the distance reduces the field to one quarter.

correct_answer: any tangential component would drive the free surface charges along the surface, so equilibrium would not have been reached
explanation: Free charges on a conductor respond to any tangential field by moving. In the final static state there can be no such motion, so the tangential component must be zero and the field is purely normal to the surface.

In a medium the permittivity is epsilon = K ε₀, so the field becomes E' = q / (4 π K ε₀ r²) = E / K. With K = 2 the field is halved. Physically, the medium polarises and the induced bound charges partly oppose the field of the free charge.

Each charge contributes 2 k q / a² times cos 45, that is √2 k q / a², and all four contributions point the same way, giving 4 √2 k q / a² directed from the positive pair towards the negative pair.
Writing E = (k q) × (1 / r²) shows that E is directly proportional to 1 / r². A plot of E against 1 / r² is therefore a straight line through the origin with slope k q.

correct_answer: the electric field would have two different directions at the same point
explanation: The tangent to a line of force at any point gives the direction of the electric field there. If two lines crossed, two different tangents would exist at the crossing point, so the field would have two directions at once. Since the force on a test charge at a point is unique, this is impossible.

Both particles carry the same magnitude of charge, so both experience the same magnitude of force q E in the same field. Since a = F / m, the accelerations are inversely proportional to the masses, giving a_electron / a_proton = m_proton / m_electron, about 1836. The two fields are at right angles, so the resultant has magnitude √(300² + 400²) = √(90000 + 160000) = √(250000) = 500 N C⁻¹. Its direction makes an angle whose tangent is 4/3 with the easterly field.
a = 1 × 10⁻⁶ x 1000 / (1 × 10⁻³) = 1 m s⁻². The time to cover 1 m along the initial direction is t = 1 / 10 = 0.1 s. The sideways displacement is y = 0.5 × 1 × (0.1)² = 5 × 10⁻³ m = 5 mm.

The centre is equidistant from all four corners, so each charge produces a field of the same magnitude there. correct_answer: start on positive charges and end on negative charges
explanation: A positive test charge is pushed away from a positive charge and pulled towards a negative charge. So lines of force originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges. For an isolated positive charge the lines run outward to infinity.

If the field had a component along the surface, it would exert a force on the free charges and set them moving, contradicting the assumption of equilibrium. Hence the surface field can only be normal to the surface. Inside the conductor the field is zero, so no lines exist there.

correct_answer: vertically upward and of magnitude e E
explanation: The magnitude of the force is |q| E = e E. Because the electron has negative charge, the force is opposite in direction to the field, so a downward field pushes an electron upward.

correct_answer: 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ both before and after the replacement
explanation: E = 0.1 / (2 × 10⁻⁶) = 5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. The field at a point is created by the source charges and does not depend on the size or sign of the charge used to probe it, so it is unchanged when the test charge is replaced. Only the force on the new charge changes.

A positive test charge placed near a negative charge is attracted, so the force on it points towards the charge. Since E has the direction of this force, the field is radially inward everywhere around a negative point charge.

Treat the hemisphere plus its flat circular face as a closed surface enclosing no charge, so the total flux is zero. The flux entering through the flat face is E times its area π R². correct_answer: E S cos(θ), measured in N m² C⁻¹
explanation: Flux counts the field lines crossing the surface. Only the component of E along the normal, that is E cos(θ), contributes, so φ = E S cos(θ). The unit is newton metre squared per coulomb, equivalently volt metre.

Flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀ and is completely independent of the radius. correct_answer: a scalar quantity that can be positive, negative or zero
explanation: Flux is defined as the scalar product of the field and the area vector, so it is a scalar. Its sign depends on the angle θ: it is positive when lines leave the surface, negative when they enter, and zero when the field lies in the plane of the surface.

correct_answer: zero, although the field on the surface is not zero
explanation: The total flux depends only on the net charge inside. With no enclosed charge the net flux is zero. This does not make the field zero on the surface: field lines from outside charges enter on one side and leave on the other, so the incoming negative flux exactly cancels the outgoing positive flux.

correct_answer: lies entirely in the plane of the surface

correct_answer: The field can be zero where the potential is not zero, and the potential can be zero where the field is not zero
explanation: At the midpoint between two equal positive charges the fields cancel while the potentials add, so E = 0 and V is not zero. correct_answer: the potential is zero while the electric field is not zero
explanation: An equatorial point is equidistant from the two charges, so the positive and negative contributions to the potential, which are scalars, cancel exactly. correct_answer: perpendicular to the electric field lines at every point
explanation: Moving a charge along an equipotential surface involves no change of potential and hence no work. Since the work equals q E times the displacement along E, the field must have no component along the surface, so it is perpendicular to the surface everywhere.

correct_answer: 20 N C⁻¹ directed along the negative x direction
explanation: dV/dx = 10 x, so E = -10 x. At x = 2 m, E = -20 N C⁻¹, that is a field of magnitude 20 N C⁻¹ pointing in the negative x direction, towards lower potential.

correct_answer: the electric field is zero everywhere

correct_answer: along the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly
explanation: The negative sign in E = -dV/dr means the field points from higher to lower potential, and its magnitude equals the maximum rate at which the potential falls with distance.

correct_answer: is a horizontal straight line up to r = R and then falls off as 1 / r
explanation: Inside the conductor the field is zero, so the potential does not change and stays at its surface value k Q / R, giving a flat portion of the graph. correct_answer: the proton moves towards regions of lower potential and the electron towards regions of higher potential
explanation: Every free particle moves so as to lower its own potential energy U = q V. correct_answer: adding the individual potentials algebraically with their signs
explanation: Potential is energy per unit charge and therefore a scalar. Contributions from different charges add algebraically, positive for positive charges and negative for negative charges. This is why potentials are far easier to combine than fields, which require vector addition.

correct_answer: the field is zero and the potential equals the potential at the surface

correct_answer: volt, equal to one joule per coulomb

correct_answer: the electric field is zero while the potential has twice the value due to one charge

correct_answer: sigma / (2 ε₀), the same at all distances from the sheet
explanation: A cylindrical Gaussian surface with its flat faces of area A parallel to the sheet gives 2 E A = sigma A / ε₀, so E = sigma / (2 ε₀). The result contains no distance, so the field is uniform on either side of the sheet.

correct_answer: the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by ε₀

correct_answer: sigma / ε₀ between the sheets and zero outside them
