Diamagnetism arises from a change induced by the field in the orbital motion of paired electrons. This change does not compete with thermal agitation, because there are no permanent dipoles to be disturbed. Hence the diamagnetic susceptibility is practically independent of temperature.

The field inside is B = μ₀ (1 + chi) H. For this to vanish for any non zero H, we need 1 + chi = 0, that is chi = -1. Then mu_r = 1 + chi = 0. A superconductor is therefore described as a perfect diamagnet, with the most negative susceptibility physically possible.

First M = chi H = (-1.5 × 10⁻⁵) × (1 × 10⁵) = -1.5 A m⁻¹. The total moment is then m_net = M V = -1.5 × 1 × 10⁻³ = -1.5 × 10⁻³ A m², whose magnitude is 1.5 × 10⁻³ A m², directed opposite to the applied field.

correct_answer: the orbital and spin moments of the electrons cancel, leaving no net atomic moment
explanation: In a diamagnetic substance all the electrons are paired, so the orbital and spin contributions add vectorially to zero and each atom has no permanent magnetic moment. When a field is applied, the electronic motion is modified so as to produce an induced moment opposing the field.
mu_r = 1 + chi = 1 - 4 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.99996. Hence B = 0.99996 × 1 = 0.99996 T. The field inside is thus very slightly less than the applied field, a change of only four parts in a hundred thousand.

Since chi for a diamagnetic substance is about -10⁻⁵, the relative permeability mu_r = 1 + chi is slightly less than one, typically about 0.99999. Hence the field inside such a substance is a little weaker than the applied field.

correct_answer: oppositely directed, so the susceptibility is negative and very small in magnitude
explanation: An applied field induces atomic moments in a diamagnetic substance that oppose the field, so M points opposite to H and chi = M / H is negative. The induced moments are tiny, so the magnitude of chi is only about 10⁻⁵.

correct_answer: X moves towards the weaker field while Y moves towards the stronger field
explanation: The diamagnetic sphere acquires a moment opposing the field, so the force on it drives it towards the region of weaker field. The paramagnetic sphere acquires a moment along the field, so it is drawn towards the region of stronger field. Both forces are feeble because the magnitudes of the susceptibilities are only about 10⁻⁵.

correct_answer: from the region of stronger field towards the region of weaker field
explanation: The induced moment in a diamagnetic sample is antiparallel to the field. The energy of such a dipole is least where the field is weakest, so the sample is pushed from the stronger towards the weaker part of the field. Placed between the poles of an electromagnet, a diamagnetic rod moves outwards from the gap.

Bismuth is the standard example of a strongly diamagnetic solid; copper, gold, water, lead and silver behave similarly. Aluminium and platinum have unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic, while nickel is ferromagnetic.

Since the magnetisation of a diamagnetic specimen opposes the applied field, the resultant field inside it is slightly weaker than the applied field, that is B = mu_r B₀ with mu_r slightly less than one. This shows up as a slight expulsion of the lines of the field from the specimen.

correct_answer: opposite to the applied field, so as to oppose the change producing it
explanation: Switching on the field changes the flux through the electronic orbits. The orbital motion adjusts so as to oppose that change, exactly in the spirit of Lenz law, and the resulting induced moment points opposite to the applied field. This is why the magnetisation and hence the susceptibility are negative.

The field of the magnet induces in the diamagnetic sample a magnetic moment directed opposite to itself. A dipole opposing the field is pushed towards weaker field, so the sample is weakly repelled by the pole of the magnet.

correct_answer: a small region in which the atomic magnetic moments are spontaneously aligned in one direction
explanation: In a ferromagnetic material a strong interaction between neighbouring atoms lines up their magnetic moments over small regions called domains, each containing a very large number of atoms. In an unmagnetised sample the domains point in different directions so that the moments cancel overall.

correct_answer: greatest for the specimen with susceptibility 2 × 10³
explanation: The magnetisation acquired is M = chi H, and the force in a non uniform field is proportional to this induced moment. The specimen with chi = 2 × 10³ acquires a magnetisation about ten million times larger than the others, so it experiences by far the greatest force. Its positive sign also means the force is an attraction.

The common ferromagnetic elements are iron, cobalt, nickel and gadolinium, all of which show spontaneous alignment of atomic moments within domains. Manganese and oxygen are paramagnetic and copper is diamagnetic.

correct_answer: is not a constant, since the magnetisation depends on the previous magnetic history of the sample
explanation: The magnetisation of a ferromagnetic sample rises steeply and then saturates, and on reversing the field it lags behind, so the same value of H can correspond to different values of M. The ratio chi = M / H therefore varies along the curve and even depends on the previous magnetic history of the sample.

correct_answer: very much greater than one, often several thousand
explanation: Since chi for a ferromagnetic material runs into thousands, mu_r = 1 + chi is very much greater than one. Soft iron, for instance, may have a relative permeability of several thousand, which is why it multiplies the field of a solenoid so strongly.
The magnetic intensity is H = N I / L = 500 × 1 / 0.5 = 1000 A m⁻¹. The susceptibility is chi = mu_r - 1 = 999. Hence M = chi H = 999 × 1000 = 999000 A m⁻¹, that is nearly 9.99 × 10⁵ A m⁻¹.

The field of the magnet causes the domains of the ferromagnetic piece to grow and rotate, giving it a very large magnetisation along the field. This large induced moment is then drawn strongly towards the region of stronger field, that is towards the pole.

correct_answer: domains favourably oriented with respect to the field grow at the expense of the others
explanation: In a weak field the boundaries between domains move so that domains already pointing near the direction of the field grow at the expense of unfavourably oriented ones. In stronger fields the moments of whole domains rotate into the direction of the field. Together these give the very large magnetisation of a ferromagnetic specimen.

correct_answer: positive and very large, running into thousands
explanation: In a ferromagnetic material the atomic dipoles inside a domain are already aligned by a strong internal interaction, so even a modest applied field produces an enormous magnetisation. The susceptibility chi = M / H is therefore positive and very large, typically of the order of 10³ or more.
For a single turn the field at the centre varies inversely as the first power of the radius. Doubling R therefore halves the field at the centre.

For one turn of radius R the field is μ₀ I / (2 R). For two turns each of radius R / 2 the field is μ₀ x 2 x I / (2 x R / 2) = 2 μ₀ I / R. Dividing, the second field is 4 times the first. In general, rewinding a fixed length into N turns multiplies the centre field by N².

The 10 cm loop gives (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10) / (2 × 0.10) = 2 π x 10⁻⁵ T, about 6.28 × 10⁻⁵ T. The 5 cm loop gives (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10) / (2 × 0.05) = 4 π x 10⁻⁵ T, about 1.26 × 10⁻⁴ T. Since the planes are perpendicular, the two axial fields are perpendicular, so the resultant is 2 π x 10⁻⁵ x square root of (1 + 4) = 2 π square root of 5 × 10⁻⁵ T, which is about 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ T.

A semicircle is half of a full turn, so the field at the centre is half of μ₀ I / (2 R), that is μ₀ I / (4 R). Substituting, B = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 4) / (4 × 0.10) = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 4) / 0.40 = 4 π x 10⁻⁶ T, about 1.26 × 10⁻⁵ T.

The inner arc gives (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10) / (4 × 0.10) = 10 π x 10⁻⁶ T. The outer arc gives (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10) / (4 × 0.20) = 5 π x 10⁻⁶ T. Both arcs are traversed in the same sense, so their axial fields point the same way and add to 15 π x 10⁻⁶ T, that is about 4.7 × 10⁻⁵ T. The radial pieces pass through the centre line and contribute nothing.

correct_answer: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a north pole
explanation: Curling the right hand fingers along the current, the thumb points out of the face from which the current looks anticlockwise. The field emerges from that face, so it acts as the north pole, while the other face, where the current looks clockwise, acts as the south pole.
Dividing, B_axis / B_centre = R³ / (R² + x²)³⁄². With x = R this becomes R³ / (2 R²)³⁄² = R³ / (2³⁄² R³) = 1 / (2 square root of 2), which is about 0.354.

When x is much greater than R, the term R² in the bracket may be neglected, giving B = μ₀ I R² / (2 x³). Writing the magnetic moment as m = I π R², this becomes B = μ₀ x 2 m / (4 π x³), the standard axial field of a magnetic dipole, which falls off as the cube of the distance.

correct_answer: 8 square root of 2 : pi², that is about 1.15 : 1
explanation: For the circle, 2 π R = L gives R = L / (2 π), so B_circle = μ₀ I / (2 R) = π μ₀ I / L. For the square, 4 a = L gives a = L / 4. Each side is a finite wire whose perpendicular distance from the centre is a / 2, and each side subtends 45° on either side of that perpendicular. One side therefore gives (μ₀ I / (4 π x a / 2)) × (sin 45 + sin 45) = (μ₀ I / (2 π a)) x square root of 2. Four sides give B_square = 2 square root of 2 μ₀ I / (π a) = 8 square root of 2 μ₀ I / (π L). Dividing, B_square / B_circle = 8 square root of 2 / pi² = 11.31 / 9.87 = 1.15. The square gives the slightly stronger central field because parts of it lie closer to the centre.

Every element of the loop is at the same distance R from the centre and every element makes an angle of 90° with the line to the centre, so the contributions add directly to give B = μ₀ I / (2 R) for one turn, and N times this for N turns.
With the radius and current unchanged, B is directly proportional to N. Increasing N from 1 to 50 therefore increases the field fifty fold, giving 50 B.
An arc of 60° is one sixth of a full circle, so it contributes one sixth of the full loop field: B = (1 / 6) x μ₀ I / (2 R) = μ₀ I / (12 R).
Here square root of (3² + 4²) = 5 cm, so the ratio is 3³ / 5³ = 27 / 125. Hence B_axis = 125 × 10⁻⁶ x 27 / 125 = 27 × 10⁻⁶ T.

correct_answer: out of the plane of the paper, towards the reader
explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand along the anticlockwise current; the extended thumb then points out of the paper. Hence the field at the centre, and everywhere on the axis, is directed out of the plane of the loop towards the reader. That face of the loop behaves as a north pole.

The inner loop gives μ₀ I / (2 R) and the outer loop gives μ₀ I / (2 × 2 R) = μ₀ I / (4 R). Because the currents circulate in opposite senses, the two axial fields are oppositely directed, so the resultant is μ₀ I / (2 R) minus μ₀ I / (4 R) = μ₀ I / (4 R), in the sense of the inner loop.
Since B = μ₀ I / (2 π r), the field varies inversely as the first power of r. Doubling the distance from 4 cm to 8 cm therefore halves the field, giving B / 2.

correct_answer: The magnitude of B is the same at every point of a circle drawn around the wire in a perpendicular plane, but its direction changes from point to point
explanation: The magnitude depends only on r, so all points of a given circle have equal field strength. The direction is tangential to that circle, so it rotates continuously as one moves around the circle. This constancy of magnitude with a tangential direction is precisely what makes such a circle a convenient Amperian loop.

Integrating the Biot Savart law along an infinite straight wire gives B = μ₀ I / (2 π r). The field falls off as the first power of the distance, not as its square, because contributions come from the whole length of the wire.

Each wire is 0.10 m from P, so each contributes 2 × 10⁻⁷ x 10 / 0.10 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T. Each field is perpendicular to the line joining that wire to P. Since the wires and P form an equilateral triangle and the currents are oppositely directed, the two field vectors turn out to be inclined at 120° to each other. For two equal vectors of magnitude B at 120°, the resultant magnitude is B square root of (1 + 1 + 2 cos 120) = B. Hence the resultant is 2 × 10⁻⁵ T, directed perpendicular to the line joining the two wires.

correct_answer: zero, since every current element of the conductor makes an angle of 0° or 180° with the line to that point
explanation: Each element I dl of the conductor and the line joining it to the given point are collinear, so θ is 0° or 180° and sin θ = 0. Every element contributes zero, so the resultant field at such a point is zero.

For wire P, B_P = μ₀ I / (2 π r). For wire Q, B_Q = μ₀ (2 I) / (2 π x 2 r) = μ₀ I / (2 π r). The doubling of the current is exactly cancelled by the doubling of the distance, so the two fields are the same.

correct_answer: 10 cm to the west of the wire
explanation: For cancellation the wire must produce a field of 4 × 10⁻⁵ T pointing south. Equating magnitudes, 2 × 10⁻⁷ x 20 / r = 4 × 10⁻⁵, so r = 4 × 10⁻⁶ / 4 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.10 m = 10 cm. For an upward current, the circular field lines run anticlockwise when seen from above, so the field points south only on the western side of the wire. Hence the point is 10 cm to the west.

Each wire is 0.10 m from the midpoint, so each produces B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ x 5 / 0.10 = 1 × 10⁻⁵ T. For currents in opposite directions the two fields at a point between the wires point the same way, so they add: B = 1 × 10⁻⁵ + 1 × 10⁻⁵ = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T.

Take the current along the upward vertical and the point to the east. The field direction is given by the vector product of the upward direction with the eastward radial direction, which points to the north. Equivalently, curling the right hand fingers around the upward thumb sends the field anticlockwise seen from above, which is northward on the eastern side.

correct_answer: concentric circles lying in planes perpendicular to the wire, with the sense given by the right hand thumb rule
explanation: Point the right thumb along the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers then give the sense in which the circular field lines are traced. These circles lie in planes at right angles to the wire, centred on the wire.
B = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 5) / (2 π x 0.10). The factor π cancels, leaving B = (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 5) / 0.10 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.10 = 1 × 10⁻⁵ T.
Substituting unit currents and unit separation, F / l = (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 1 × 1) / 1 = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹. This is precisely the value used to define the ampere.

The upper wire must be pushed upward, so the magnetic force between the wires must be repulsive, which requires the two currents to flow in opposite directions. Equating the repulsive force per unit length to the weight per unit length gives (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 100 x I) / 0.01 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ x 10. The left side is 2 × 10⁻³ I and the right side is 5 × 10⁻³, so I = 2.5 A.

correct_answer: zero, because the vector sum of the length elements around a closed loop is zero
explanation: The total force is the sum of I dl x B over the loop. Since B is the same at every point, it can be taken outside, leaving I (sum of dl) x B. The vector sum of the length elements around any closed path is zero, so the net force vanishes for a loop of any shape. A net torque may nevertheless act, which is what makes motors work.

Wire A attracts B with (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 10 × 20) / 0.10 = 4 × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹ towards A. Wire C attracts B with (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 20 × 30) / 0.10 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹ towards C. These pulls are in opposite directions, so the net force per unit length is 1.2 × 10⁻³ minus 4 × 10⁻⁴ = 8 × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹, directed towards C.

The force per unit length is proportional to I1 and inversely proportional to d. Doubling I1 doubles it and halving d doubles it again, so the product of the two factors gives four times the original value.

In a uniform field the force on a bent conductor depends only on the vector joining its ends, since F = I (sum of dl) x B and the sum of dl is that joining vector. For a semicircle the ends are separated by the diameter, so L_effective = 2 R = 0.4 m. Hence F = 0.4 × 5 × 0.4 = 0.8 N, directed along the perpendicular bisector of the diameter.

Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other. Applying the rule for the force on a current carrying conductor shows that for currents in the same direction the forces pull the wires together, while for currents in opposite directions they push them apart.

correct_answer: B I l sin θ, and it is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field
explanation: The force is the vector product I (l x B), of magnitude B I l sin θ. It is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field and vanishes when the conductor lies along the field, since then sin θ = 0.

The component of velocity along the field is v cos 60 = 4 × 10⁵ x 0.5 = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, and this component is unaffected by the field. The period is T = 2 π m / (q B) = 2 π x 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 0.2) = 2 π x 5 × 10⁻⁸ = 3.14 × 10⁻⁷ s. The pitch is 2 × 10⁵ x 3.14 × 10⁻⁷ = 6.28 × 10⁻² m, about 6.3 cm.

The magnetic force is the vector product q (v x B), whose magnitude is q v B sin θ. It is greatest when the velocity is perpendicular to the field and zero when the velocity is parallel or antiparallel to it.

For undeflected motion the electric and magnetic forces must balance: q E = q v B, giving v = E / B = (3 × 10⁴) / 0.06 = 5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. The selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass of the particle.

Entering normally, the ion turns on a circle whose centre lies on the entry face. The greatest perpendicular distance it can reach from that face is one radius, attained after it has turned through 90°. The condition for emerging is sin θ = d / r with θ less than 90°, that is d less than r. If d is equal to or greater than r, the ion curves back and returns through the face by which it entered.

correct_answer: The proton describes the larger circle, its radius being about 43 times that of the electron
explanation: Writing the momentum in terms of kinetic energy, p = square root of (2 m K), so r = square root of (2 m K) / (q B). For equal K and equal charge magnitude, r is proportional to the square root of the mass. The proton is about 1836 times as massive as the electron, so its radius is larger by the square root of 1836, which is about 43.

Taking east as the first vector and north as the second, the vector product of east with north points vertically upward. Since the charge is positive, the force is along that direction, that is vertically upward.
The selected speed is v = E / B = (2 × 10⁴) / 0.1 = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. In the analysing field, m / q = r B' / v = (0.1 × 0.2) / (2 × 10⁵) = 0.02 / (2 × 10⁵) = 1 × 10⁻⁷ kg C⁻¹.

correct_answer: the period of revolution is unchanged and the radius of the path is doubled
explanation: The radius r = m v / (q B) is proportional to the speed, so doubling v doubles r. The period T = 2 π r / v = 2 π m / (q B) contains no v at all, so it is unchanged. The faster particle simply travels around a proportionately larger circle in the same time.

Acceleration through V gives v = square root of (2 q V / m), so r = m v / (q B) = square root of (2 m V / q) / B. Hence r is proportional to the square root of m / q. For the alpha particle m is 4 times and q is 2 times those of the proton, so m / q is doubled and r is larger by the square root of 2, about 1.41 times.

correct_answer: The speed and the kinetic energy of the particle remain constant while the direction of its velocity changes
explanation: Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, the work it does is zero and the kinetic energy cannot change. Only the direction of the velocity is altered, which is why the path curves.

From r = m v / (q B), the speed is v = (q / m) B r = 1 × 10⁸ x 0.4 × 0.1 = 4 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2 π m / (q B) = 2 π / (1 × 10⁸ x 0.4) = 2 π / (4 × 10⁷) = 1.57 × 10⁻⁷ s, about 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ s. As a check, 2 π r / v = 0.628 / (4 × 10⁶) gives the same period.

The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, so q v B = m v² / r. Cancelling one power of v gives r = m v / (q B). The radius is therefore proportional to the momentum and inversely proportional to the charge and the field.

correct_answer: applying a very strong field at a very low temperature
explanation: The degree of alignment depends on the ratio of the magnetic energy of a dipole in the field to the thermal energy. Making the field very strong increases the aligning energy, while lowering the temperature reduces the disordering thermal energy. Both together drive the magnetisation towards its saturation value, where every dipole is aligned.
M = chi H = 3 × 10⁻⁴ x 2 × 10⁴ = 6 × 10⁰ = 6 A m⁻¹. The magnetisation is along the magnetic intensity because the susceptibility is positive.

correct_answer: it loses its magnetisation almost at once, as thermal agitation randomises the dipoles
explanation: In a paramagnetic sample the alignment of the permanent dipoles is a balance between the aligning torque of the field and the disordering effect of thermal motion. Once the field is removed, only thermal motion is left, so the dipoles return to random directions and the magnetisation disappears almost immediately.

correct_answer: slightly stronger, since the magnetisation adds to the applied field
explanation: The magnetisation of a paramagnetic rod points along the applied field, so B = μ₀ (H + M) is a little larger than μ₀ H. Since chi is only about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³, the increase is a fraction of a per cent, which is why the field lines are only slightly more crowded inside the rod.

correct_answer: decreases, because increased thermal agitation disturbs the alignment of the atomic dipoles
explanation: The applied field tries to line the permanent atomic dipoles up along itself while thermal agitation keeps knocking them out of line. Raising the temperature strengthens the disordering effect, so the fraction aligned falls, the susceptibility falls as 1 / T and the magnetisation decreases.

If every dipole were aligned the magnetisation would be M_saturation = N mu = 5 × 10²⁸ x 2 × 10⁻²³ = 1 × 10⁶ A m⁻¹. The measured value is only 10 A m⁻¹, so the fraction aligned is 10 / (1 × 10⁶) = 1 × 10⁻⁵. This tiny fraction is why paramagnetic susceptibilities are so small.

correct_answer: are permanent but point in random directions, giving zero net magnetisation
explanation: A paramagnetic atom has unpaired electrons, so it possesses a permanent magnetic moment. Thermal agitation keeps these moments pointing in random directions, so the vector sum over any macroscopic volume is zero and the substance shows no magnetisation until a field is applied.

correct_answer: positive and small, typically between 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻³
explanation: In a paramagnetic material the permanent atomic dipoles are partially aligned along the applied field, so M is along H and chi is positive. Thermal agitation keeps the alignment very incomplete, so chi is only about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³.

Aluminium has unpaired electrons and so possesses a permanent atomic magnetic moment, which makes it paramagnetic. Platinum, manganese, chromium and oxygen behave in the same way. Copper and bismuth are diamagnetic and cobalt is ferromagnetic.

correct_answer: with its length along the direction of the field
explanation: The paramagnetic rod acquires a moment along the field. The torque on a magnetic dipole in a field vanishes and is stable when the moment lies along the field, so the rod turns until its length lies along the direction of the field.

correct_answer: The field well inside is uniform and directed along the axis, while just outside the winding it is very weak
explanation: For a long, closely wound solenoid the interior field is uniform, axial and equal to μ₀ n I at all interior points, while the exterior field is very small because the return flux spreads over a large region. This makes a solenoid the practical way of producing a uniform magnetic field.
n = B / (μ₀ I) = (4 π x 10⁻³) / (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 5) = (10⁴) / 5 = 2000 turns per metre. Since the length is 1 m, the total number of turns required is 2000.

correct_answer: zero in the empty space inside the inner radius and zero outside the toroid, and non zero only within the core enclosed by the windings
explanation: A circular loop drawn inside the inner radius encloses no current, so B = 0 there. A loop drawn outside the whole toroid is threaded by each turn twice, once inward and once outward, so the net enclosed current is zero and B = 0 there too. Only a loop lying within the core is threaded by N turns, giving B = μ₀ N I / (2 π r).

correct_answer: The field inside a long solenoid is uniform, whereas across the cross section of a toroid the field varies as 1 / r and so is not strictly uniform
explanation: In a long solenoid the interior field is μ₀ n I everywhere, independent of position and of radius. In a toroid, the same Amperian argument gives B = μ₀ N I / (2 π r), so points nearer the inner edge of the core have a stronger field than points nearer the outer edge. The field is nearly uniform only when the cross section is small compared with the mean radius.

correct_answer: doubling the current while keeping the number of turns per unit length unchanged
explanation: Since B = μ₀ n I, the interior field is doubled by doubling either the current or the number of turns per unit length. Doubling the length at fixed total turns halves n and therefore halves B, while changing the radius or the leads has no effect.

Stretching at constant N doubles L, so n = N / L is halved. Since B = μ₀ n I and I is unchanged, the field is halved.
At the middle, turns lie on both sides and contribute fully. At the end, only half the winding lies on one side, so the axial field is halved: B_end = μ₀ n I / 2.

correct_answer: the plane of the coil always contains the field, so the deflecting torque is N B I A for every position and the scale becomes linear
explanation: In a radial field the field lines are always parallel to the plane of the coil, so sin θ = 1 whatever the deflection. correct_answer: Increasing the number of turns raises the current sensitivity, but since the resistance of the coil also rises, the voltage sensitivity need not increase

explanation: The first minima on the two sides are each at λ x D / a from the centre, so the central band spans 2 x λ x D / a. Successive minima are separated by λ x D / a, so each secondary maximum is only half as wide, and its peak intensity is a small fraction of the central one.

correct_answer: 90°, so no minimum is seen and the light spreads over the whole forward region
explanation: With a = λ, sin θ = λ / λ = 1, so θ = 90°. The first minimum is pushed to the edge of the forward hemisphere, which means the central maximum fills the entire region beyond the slit and no dark band is observed.

correct_answer: the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable with the wavelength of the light
explanation: The half angular width of the central maximum is λ / a. For visible light of about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m passing an aperture of a few millimetres this angle is only about 10⁻⁴ radian, which is too small to notice, but for an aperture of the order of a micrometre it becomes large.

correct_answer: a x sin θ = n x λ, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on
explanation: The slit is imagined as split into pairs of strips whose contributions cancel in pairs when the extreme path difference a x sin θ equals a whole number of wavelengths. The value n = 0 must be excluded because there all the strips arrive in step, giving the central maximum.

correct_answer: bending of light around the edges of an obstacle or an aperture into the region of the geometrical shadow
explanation: When a wavefront is partly blocked, the secondary wavelets from the exposed part spread sideways, so light appears inside the region that geometrical optics would call a shadow.

correct_answer: the amplitude of a secondary wavelet is maximum in the forward direction and falls to zero in the backward direction
explanation: The strength of a secondary wavelet depends on the angle θ measured from the forward normal. It is greatest at θ = 0° and becomes zero at θ = 180°, so no backward travelling wavefront is produced.
λ inside glass = 6000 / 1.5 = 4000 Å.

correct_answer: speed decreases, wavelength decreases, frequency remains the same
explanation: The frequency is set by the source and is the same in every medium. Since v = c / mu is smaller in glass and v = f x λ, the wavelength in glass must be λ divided by mu, that is smaller than in air.
Extra optical path = (1.5 minus 1) × 6 cm = 0.5 × 6 = 3 cm = 3 × 10⁻² m. With λ = 6000 Å = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m, the number of wavelengths = (3 × 10⁻²) / (6 × 10⁻⁷) = 5 × 10⁴.
Speed in glass v = (3 × 10⁸) / 1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m per second. Thickness = 3 cm = 3 × 10⁻² m. Time t = (3 × 10⁻²) / (2 × 10⁸) = 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ s.

correct_answer: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
explanation: In the construction the distance travelled by the wavelet from the first point and the distance travelled by the incident wavefront to reach the mirror are both v x t. The two right triangles formed share the same hypotenuse and have equal perpendiculars, so they are congruent and the two angles are equal.

correct_answer: the common tangent, that is the envelope, to all the secondary wavelets
explanation: Each point of the old wavefront emits a wavelet of radius v x t. The surface that touches all of these wavelets in the forward direction is the new wavefront at that instant.
mu = (3 × 10⁸) / (1.5 × 10⁸) = 2. Wavelength inside the liquid = 6000 / 2 = 3000 Å. The frequency stays 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz in both media.
mu = sin 45° divided by sin 30° = (1 divided by square root of 2) divided by (1 divided by 2) = 2 divided by square root of 2 = square root of 2, about 1.41.

correct_answer: v1 / v2, which equals mu2 / mu1
explanation: In the construction the incident wavefront covers v1 x t along the surface while the refracted wavelet covers v2 x t inside medium 2. Dividing the two sine expressions built on the common hypotenuse gives sin i / sin r = v1 / v2, and since mu = c / v this equals mu2 / mu1.

correct_answer: the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them
explanation: The positions of the maxima depend on the phase difference between the arriving waves. Only if that phase difference is fixed do the maxima stay at the same places long enough for the eye to see a steady pattern.

correct_answer: destructively, the phase difference being 3 π radian
explanation: Phase difference = (2 x π / λ) × 1.5 λ = 3 π radian. Since 3 π is an odd multiple of π, the two equal displacements are exactly opposite and the resultant amplitude is zero, so the point is dark.
I = I0 plus I0 plus 2 x square root of (I0 x I0) x cos 90° = 2 I0 plus 2 I0 × 0 = 2 I0.
Phase difference = (2 x π / λ) × (λ / 3) = 2 π / 3, that is 120°. Then I = Imax x cos² 60° = Imax x 0.25 = Imax / 4.
A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths corresponds to a phase difference of 2 x π x n, so the two displacements are in step and the amplitudes add.

correct_answer: phase difference = (2 x π / λ) x path difference
explanation: One full wavelength of path difference corresponds to one complete cycle, that is 2 x π radian. Scaling in proportion gives phase difference = (2 x π / λ) x path difference.
Taking square roots, (a1 plus a2) / (a1 minus a2) = 5 / 3. Cross multiplying gives 3 a1 plus 3 a2 = 5 a1 minus 5 a2, so 8 a2 = 2 a1 and a1 / a2 = 4. Hence I1 / I2 = 4² = 16 : 1.
Phase difference = (2 x π / λ) × (λ / 4) = 2 x π / 4 = π / 2 radian, which is 90°.

correct_answer: The two sources must be coherent and must emit light of the same wavelength
explanation: If the sources are not coherent the positions of the maxima shift randomly, and if the wavelengths differ the two patterns of different fringe width overlap. Both conditions must hold for a steady visible pattern.
Amplitudes are in the ratio 1 : 2, so Imax is proportional to (1 plus 2)² = 9 and Imin is proportional to (2 minus 1)² = 1. Then (9 minus 1) divided by (9 plus 1) = 8 / 10 = 4 / 5.

correct_answer: the two lamps emit light in independent bursts, so the phase difference between them changes randomly and very rapidly
explanation: Atoms in each lamp radiate independently in wave trains lasting about 10⁻⁸ s. The phase relation between the two lamps therefore changes millions of times per second, so the maxima shift about far too quickly to be seen and the screen looks uniformly lit.

correct_answer: light energy is only redistributed, the total energy remaining the same
explanation: At a bright band the intensity of two equal sources rises to 4 x I0 and at a dark band it falls to zero. The average over the pattern is 2 x I0, exactly the sum of the two separate intensities, so the total energy is unchanged and only its distribution alters.
Maximum amplitude = 5a plus 3a = 8a and minimum amplitude = 5a minus 3a = 2a. Hence Imax / Imin = (8a)² / (2a)² = 64 / 4 = 16 : 1.

correct_answer: (square root of I1 minus square root of I2)², which is greater than zero
explanation: Amplitudes are proportional to the square roots of the intensities, so at destructive interference the resultant amplitude is the square root of I1 minus the square root of I2. Squaring gives the minimum intensity, which is zero only if I1 = I2.
An odd number of half wavelengths corresponds to a phase difference of an odd multiple of π, so one displacement is exactly opposite to the other and for equal amplitudes the resultant is zero.
Since amplitude is the square root of intensity, a1 : a2 = 3 : 1. Then Imax / Imin = (3 plus 1)² / (3 minus 1)² = 16 / 4 = 4 : 1.

In a longitudinal wave the vibration is along the direction of propagation, so no direction across the ray is special and polarisation is impossible. Light can be polarised by a polaroid, hence its vibrations must be perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

In time t the disturbance from the point source covers the same distance v x t in every direction, so all points in the same phase lie on a sphere of radius v x t centred on the source. The wavefront is therefore spherical.

correct_answer: The ray is always perpendicular to the wavefront at the point where it meets it
explanation: Energy travels outward along the shortest path from one wavefront to the next, which is along the normal to the wavefront. Hence the ray is drawn perpendicular to the wavefront everywhere.

The energy crossing a cylindrical surface of radius r per second is fixed, and that area is proportional to r. Hence I varies as 1 / r. Using I proportional to A² gives A² proportional to 1 / r, so A varies as 1 divided by the square root of r.

correct_answer: Light travels faster in water than in air
explanation: For water mu is about 1.33, so the wave theory speed is c divided by 1.33, which is less than c. Wave theory therefore predicts light to be slower in water than in air, and the experiment of Foucault confirmed this.

correct_answer: only a very small portion of the enormous spherical wavefront reaches the Earth and its curvature is negligible
explanation: The radius of the wavefront at the Earth is of the order of the star distance, which is enormous. A tiny patch of a sphere whose radius is huge has almost zero curvature, so it is treated as a plane wavefront.

correct_answer: acts as a secondary source and sends out secondary wavelets in the forward direction
explanation: The disturbance reaching a point sets it vibrating, and that vibrating point radiates fresh spherical wavelets into the medium ahead. Drawing the common tangent to these forward wavelets after time t gives the wavefront at that later instant.

correct_answer: the locus of all points of the medium that vibrate in the same phase
explanation: Every point on a wavefront is reached by the disturbance at the same instant, so all such points oscillate in the same phase. Hence a wavefront is the locus of points having the same phase of vibration.

correct_answer: the speed in water is less than that in air, supporting the wave theory
explanation: Wave theory requires the speed in water to be c divided by 1.33, that is about 2.25 × 10⁸ m per second, which is smaller than 3 × 10⁸ m per second. Measurement gave the smaller value, so the wave theory prediction was confirmed.

correct_answer: along the normals to the wavefront
explanation: Successive wavefronts are separated by the shortest distance along their common normal, and the disturbance moves from one to the next along that normal. Hence the flow of energy is along the rays, which are the normals to the wavefront.

Each point of the slit sends out light; the set of points reached in the same time lies at a constant perpendicular distance from the line of the slit. That surface is a cylinder with the slit as its axis.
M = f_o / f_e = 100/5 = 20. A telescope needs a long focus objective and a short focus eyepiece for high magnification.

At the near point M = 1 + 25/5 = 6, while for the image at infinity M = 25/5 = 5. The difference is exactly one, and it is the same for any focal length because the two expressions differ only by the added one. The infinity setting is preferred for long observation because the eye is relaxed.
Objective magnification is inversely related to its focal length for a given tube length.

correct_answer: a real, inverted and magnified intermediate image
explanation: The objective forms a real enlarged intermediate image that acts as the object for the eyepiece.
Normal adjustment places the objective's real image at the eyepiece focal plane, so emerging rays are parallel.
The magnitude is f_o/f_e = 100/5 = 20.
The magnifications of objective and eyepiece multiply: 20×5 = 100.
Reflection is essentially independent of wavelength, so mirrors avoid chromatic aberration.

After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2. After the second it is (I0 / 2) x cos² 30° = (I0 / 2) × 3 / 4 = 3 I0 / 8. After the third it is (3 I0 / 8) x cos² 30° = (3 I0 / 8) × 3 / 4 = 9 I0 / 32.

correct_answer: square root of 3, that is about 1.73, and about 1.73 × 10⁸ m per second
explanation: Since the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular at the polarising angle, θ B = 90° minus 30° = 60°. Then mu = tan 60° = square root of 3, about 1.73, and v = (3 × 10⁸) divided by 1.73 = about 1.73 × 10⁸ m per second.

At the polarising angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so the angle of refraction is 90° minus θ B. Putting this in Snell law, mu = sin θ B divided by sin (90° minus θ B) = sin θ B divided by cos θ B = tan θ B.
tan of θ B = square root of 3, and since tan 60° = square root of 3, the polarising angle is 60°.

correct_answer: the angle whose sine is 1 divided by the square root of 3, that is about 35°
explanation: From Brewster law, mu = tan 60° = square root of 3, about 1.73. Then sin of the critical angle = 1 divided by 1.73 = 0.577, so the critical angle is about 35°.
After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2 and the light is plane polarised. The second polaroid then gives (I0 / 2) x cos² 90° = (I0 / 2) × 0 = 0.
After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2. The second polaroid gives (I0 / 2) x cos² 60° = (I0 / 2) × 0.25 = I0 / 8.

After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2. After the middle polaroid at 45° it is (I0 / 2) x cos² 45° = I0 / 4. The last polaroid is at 45° to the middle one, so the final intensity is (I0 / 4) x cos² 45° = I0 / 8.

correct_answer: the vibrations of the electric field are confined to a single plane containing the direction of propagation
explanation: Unpolarised light contains vibrations in every direction perpendicular to the ray. A polariser removes all of these except those parallel to one direction, so the surviving vibrations lie in a single plane that contains the ray.
r = 90° minus 60° = 30°. As a check, mu = sin 60° divided by sin 30° = square root of 3, which is also tan 60°.

The incident vibrations are spread uniformly over all directions perpendicular to the ray, so the average value of cos² of the angle is 1 / 2. The transmitted intensity is therefore I0 / 2, whatever the orientation of the polaroid.

The refractive index of glass increases as the wavelength decreases, so violet, having the shortest visible wavelength, has the largest refractive index. Since deviation increases with refractive index, violet is deviated most and red least.
Rearranging A + D = i + e gives D = i + e - A = 45 + 55 - 60 = 40°.
Angular dispersion = (1.66 - 1.62) × 5 = 0.04 × 5 = 0.2°. Individually the violet is deviated by 0.66 × 5 = 3.3° and the red by 0.62 × 5 = 3.1°, whose difference is 0.2°.
ω = (1.66 - 1.62)/(1.64 - 1) = 0.04/0.64 = 0.0625. Dispersive power is a pure number depending only on the material, not on the refracting angle of the prism.

The eyes are at 180 - 10 = 170 cm above the floor. A ray from the feet reaches the eye after reflecting at a point midway in height between the feet and the eye, that is at 170 / 2 = 85 cm above the floor. So the lower edge of the mirror must be at 85 cm. The upper edge lies midway between the eye and the top of the head, at 175 cm, giving a mirror length of 175 - 85 = 90 cm as expected.

The normal is perpendicular to the mirror surface. A ray making 30° with the surface makes 90 - 30 = 60° with the normal, so the angle of incidence is 60°. By the law of reflection the angle of reflection is also 60°.

The mirror is at rest, so v_image = -v_object with respect to the mirror. The boy moves towards the mirror at 2 m s⁻¹ and the image moves towards the mirror at 2 m s⁻¹ from the other side. Their approach speed is 2 + 2 = 4 m s⁻¹.
Five images require n - 1 = 5, so n = 6. Then θ = 360 / 6 = 60°. A check confirms 360 / 60 = 6 is even, so the rule n - 1 applies and gives 5 images.

correct_answer: P is correct and Q is wrong
explanation: A plane mirror always gives a virtual erect image of the same size as the object, so P is correct. Lateral inversion is a reversal of the front to back direction which appears as a left to right exchange; the image stays erect and is not turned upside down, so Q is wrong.

The net deviation is 360 - 2 × 70 = 220°. Turning through 220° in one sense is the same as turning through 360 - 220 = 140° in the other, so the angle between the incident and emergent rays is 140°, which equals 2 × 70. A useful check is the right angle case, where 2 × 90 = 180° gives the antiparallel ray.

When the mirror turns by 10° the normal also turns by 10°, so the angle of incidence changes by 10°. The reflected ray is measured on the other side of the normal, so its direction changes by 10° from the change in angle plus 10° from the turning of the normal, a total of 20°.

correct_answer: antiparallel to the original incident ray
explanation: With θ = 90° the total deviation is 360 - 180 = 180°. A deviation of 180° means the emergent ray travels back exactly opposite to the incident ray, that is antiparallel to it. This is the principle of a corner reflector.

Rays from the top of the head and from the feet reach the eye after reflection at points midway in height between the eye and those extremes. The mirror therefore needs to span only half the height of the person, that is 1.8 / 2 = 0.9 m. The result does not depend on how far the person stands.
The deviation is the angle between the original direction of travel and the final direction. With i = 25°, delta = 180 - 2 × 25 = 180 - 50 = 130°.
The image lies 40 cm behind the mirror. The object is 40 cm in front. The two are on opposite sides of the mirror, so the separation is 40 + 40 = 80 cm.

Snell law gives (4/3) sin 30 = (3/2) sin r, so (4/3)(1/2) = (3/2) sin r, that is 2/3 = (3/2) sin r and sin r = (2/3)(2/3) = 4/9. Since 4/9 is less than 1/2, the ray bends towards the normal, as expected on entering the denser medium.

Each layer of real thickness d contributes an apparent thickness d/mu. The total apparent depth is d/mu_1 + d/mu_2 = d(mu_2 + mu_1)/(mu_1 mu_2). As a check, putting mu_1 = mu_2 = mu gives 2d/mu, the standard single liquid result.
The refractive index of glass with respect to water is mu_glass / mu_water = (3/2) / (4/3) = (3/2) × (3/4) = 9/8 = 1.125. It exceeds one, confirming that glass is optically denser than water.

With water the shift is 8(1 - 3/4) = 8 × 0.25 = 2 cm. With the new liquid the shift is 8(1 - 1/1.6) = 8(1 - 0.625) = 8 × 0.375 = 3 cm. The microscope was already raised by 2 cm, so it must be raised a further 3 - 2 = 1 cm.

Inside the medium the wavelength is 600/1.5 = 400 nm = 4 × 10⁻⁷ m. The path is 6 cm = 6 × 10⁻² m. The number of waves is (6 × 10⁻²)/(4 × 10⁻⁷) = 1.5 × 10⁵. Equivalently the optical path is mu x 6 cm = 9 cm and dividing that by the air wavelength gives the same count.

correct_answer: smaller, the ray bending towards the normal
explanation: Snell law gives sin i / sin r = mu_water / mu_air = 4/3, which is greater than one. Hence sin r is less than sin i and r is less than i. A smaller angle with the normal means the ray has bent towards the normal on entering the denser medium.
The shift is t(1 - 1/mu) = 6(1 - 1/1.5) = 6(1 - 2/3) = 6 × 1/3 = 2 cm. Equivalently the slab of real thickness 6 cm looks only 6/1.5 = 4 cm thick, so the mark rises by 6 - 4 = 2 cm.

Snell law gives sin r = sin 60 / √(3) = (0.866)/(1.732) = 0.5, so r = 30°. The lateral shift is t sin(i - r)/cos r = 6 x sin 30 / cos 30 = 6 × 0.5 / 0.866 = 3.46 cm, which is 2 times the square root of 3 centimetres.
Apparent depth = real depth / mu = 4 / (4/3) = 4 × 3/4 = 3 m. The bottom appears raised by 4 - 3 = 1 m, which is why pools always look shallower than they are.

The frequency stays the same, so lambda_medium / lambda_vacuum = v / c = 1/mu. Hence lambda_medium = 600 / 1.5 = 400 nm. The light still appears the same colour to the eye because colour is set by frequency.
In vacuum the time is t/c = 3/(3 × 10⁸) = 1 × 10⁻⁸ s. Inside the slab the speed is c/mu, so the time is mu t/c = 1.5 × 10⁻⁸ s. The extra time is (mu - 1)t/c = 0.5 × 3/(3 × 10⁸) = 5 × 10⁻⁹ s.

For parallel boundaries the product mu sin θ is the same in every layer. Since the first and last media are both air with mu = 1, sin(emergent angle) = sin(incident angle), so the emergent angle is 40°. Only the total sideways displacement depends on the individual thicknesses and indices.
The rise is h(1 - 1/mu) = h(1 - 3/4) = h/4. Setting h/4 = 3 cm gives h = 12 cm. As a check the apparent depth is 12/(4/3) = 9 cm, which is 3 cm less than the real depth.

correct_answer: parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways
explanation: At the first face sin i = mu sin r and at the second face mu sin r = sin e, so sin e = sin i and e = i. The emergent ray is therefore parallel to the incident ray. It is however displaced sideways by the lateral shift t sin(i - r)/cos r.

correct_answer: 5 cm, converging like a concave mirror
explanation: For an equiconvex lens 1/f = (mu - 1)(2/R) gives 1/20 = 0.5 × 2/R = 1/R, so R = 20 cm. The silvered face acts as a mirror of focal length R/2 = 10 cm. Light crosses the lens, reflects and crosses the lens again, so the equivalent power is 1/F = 2/f_lens + 1/f_mirror = 2/20 + 1/10 = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2, giving F = 5 cm. The positive total power means it converges like a concave mirror.
For an equiconvex lens R₁ = +20 cm and R₂ = -20 cm. Then 1/f = (1.5 - 1)(1/20 - 1/(-20)) = 0.5 × (2/20) = 1/20, so f = 20 cm.
The powers add algebraically: P = 5 + (-2) = +3 D. The combination therefore behaves as a converging lens of focal length 1/3 m, about 33.3 cm.

The convex lens has P₁ = 1/0.20 = +5 D and the concave lens has P₂ = 1/(-0.25) = -4 D. The combination has P = 5 - 4 = +1 D, so F = 1/1 = 1 m = 100 cm. A positive power means the combination converges.

Take mu_1 = 1, mu_2 = 1.5, u = -30 cm and R = +10 cm. Then 1.5/v - 1/(-30) = (1.5 - 1)/10, that is 1.5/v + 0.0333 = 0.05, so 1.5/v = 0.01667 and v = 90 cm. The image lies 90 cm inside the glass, on the far side of the surface.

At the first surface mu_1 = 1, mu_2 = 1.5, u is infinite and R = +10 cm, so 1.5/v = 0.5/10 = 0.05 and v = 30 cm. This point lies 30 - 20 = 10 cm beyond the second surface, so it acts as a virtual object with u = +10 cm there. At the second surface mu_1 = 1.5, mu_2 = 1 and R = -10 cm, so 1/v - 1.5/10 = (1 - 1.5)/(-10) = 0.05, giving 1/v = 0.05 + 0.15 = 0.2 and v = 5 cm. The focus is 5 cm beyond the sphere.
Convert the focal length to metres first: f = 20 cm = 0.20 m. Then P = 1/f = 1/0.20 = 5 D. The power is positive because the lens is converging.

Here D = 100 cm and d = 20 cm, so f = (100² - 20²)/(4 × 100) = (10000 - 400)/400 = 9600/400 = 24 cm. Note that the two positions exist only when D is at least four times the focal length, which is satisfied since 4f = 96 cm is less than 100 cm.

correct_answer: as a parallel beam travelling along the principal axis
explanation: The parallel beam converges to the focus of the first lens, 20 cm beyond it. That point is 50 - 20 = 30 cm before the second lens, that is exactly at its focus, so u = -30 cm and f = +30 cm give 1/v = 1/30 - 1/30 = 0 and v is infinite. The emergent beam is therefore parallel. This is the telescopic or afocal arrangement used in a refracting telescope.
1/F = 1/10 + 1/15 = (3 + 2)/30 = 5/30 = 1/6, so F = 6 cm. The combination is more strongly converging than either lens alone, as expected when two positive powers add.

correct_answer: diverging with a focal length of 25 cm
explanation: f = 1/P = 1/(-4) = -0.25 m = -25 cm. The negative sign shows that the lens is concave and diverging, and the magnitude of the focal length is 25 cm.

A concave lens always diverges the rays, so they can only appear to come from a point on the object side. The image is therefore virtual and erect, and it always lies between the lens and the focus, making it smaller than the object.

correct_answer: a plane sheet of glass with zero power
explanation: The bracket mu_lens/mu_medium - 1 becomes 1.5/1.5 - 1 = 0, so 1/f = 0 and the focal length is infinite. There is no refraction at either surface because there is no change of refractive index, so the lens simply becomes invisible and passes light straight through.

For a real inverted image twice the size, m = v/u = -2. With u = -x this gives v = 2x. Substituting in the lens formula, 1/(2x) - 1/(-x) = 1/20, that is 1/(2x) + 1/x = 3/(2x) = 1/20, so x = 30 cm and v = 60 cm. The object to screen distance is 30 + 60 = 90 cm.

All rays of a parallel beam meet at one point in the focal plane. The chief ray through the optical centre is undeviated, so it fixes the image point at a distance f tan θ from the axis, which for small θ is f θ = 20 × 0.02 = 0.4 cm.

The Sun is effectively at infinity, so its image lies in the focal plane. correct_answer: shorter, because the refractive index is larger for violet
explanation: In the lens maker formula the power is proportional to mu minus one. Since mu is larger for violet than for red, the power is greater for violet and the focal length correspondingly shorter. The two focal points therefore separate, which is chromatic aberration along the axis.

At the concave mirror u = -40 cm and f = -20 cm, so 1/v = -1/20 + 1/40 = -1/40 and v = -40 cm. The intermediate image is 40 cm in front of the concave mirror, and therefore 100 - 40 = 60 cm in front of the convex mirror. For the convex mirror u = -60 cm and f = +20 cm, so 1/v = 1/20 + 1/60 = (3 + 1)/60 = 1/15 and v = +15 cm. The final image is virtual and lies 15 cm behind the convex mirror.
