The same result follows from x_object x_image = f², since 10 x x_image = 400 gives x_image = 40 cm from the focus, that is 40 + 20 = 60 cm from the pole.

correct_answer: erect, magnified and formed behind the mirror
explanation: Take f = -20 cm and u = -10 cm as an example. Then 1/v = -1/20 + 1/10 = 1/20, so v = +20 cm, behind the mirror, and m = -v/u = -20/(-10) = +2. The image is virtual, erect and magnified. This is the shaving mirror or make up mirror arrangement.

With u = -15 cm and f = -10 cm, 1/v = -1/10 + 1/15 = (-3 + 2)/30 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm. Differentiating the mirror formula gives dv/du = -v²/u² = -(30/15)² = -4. Hence the image speed is 4 times the object speed, that is 4 cm s⁻¹, and the minus sign shows the image moves away from the mirror as the object approaches.
For the convex mirror f = +R/2 = +15 cm and u = -30 cm. Then 1/v = 1/15 + 1/30 = (2 + 1)/30 = 3/30 = 1/10, so v = +10 cm. A positive v means the image is virtual and lies 10 cm behind the mirror.

Both object and image are in front of the mirror, so u = -60 cm and v = -20 cm. Then 1/f = -1/20 - 1/60 = (-3 - 1)/60 = -4/60 = -1/15, giving f = -15 cm. The radius of curvature is R = 2f, of magnitude 30 cm.

correct_answer: between the pole and the focus, behind the mirror
explanation: Put u = -x with x positive in 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/f + 1/x. As x tends to infinity, v tends to f, so a very distant object gives an image at the focus. As x tends to zero, v tends to zero, so an object touching the mirror gives an image at the pole. In between the image always lies between the pole and the focus, virtual, erect and diminished.

correct_answer: it always gives an erect image and covers a much wider field of view
explanation: Because the image is diminished, a large region behind the vehicle is compressed into the small mirror, giving a wide field of view. The image is also always erect, which makes it easy to interpret. The cost is that objects appear smaller and therefore farther away than they really are.

The image in a convex mirror is erect, so m = +1/5. With u = -x, m = -v/u gives v = x/5. Then 1/v + 1/u = 5/x - 1/x = 4/x = 1/f = 1/20, so x = 80 cm. Check: u = -80 gives 1/v = 1/20 + 1/80 = 5/80, v = 16 cm and m = -16/(-80) = 0.2.

For the nearer end u = -20 cm gives 1/v = -1/15 + 1/20 = (-4 + 3)/60 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm. For the farther end u = -30 cm gives 1/v = -1/15 + 1/30 = (-2 + 1)/30 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm. The image therefore stretches from 30 cm to 60 cm in front of the mirror, a length of 60 - 30 = 30 cm.

correct_answer: travel parallel to the principal axis
explanation: By the reversibility of light rays, since a parallel beam converges to the focus, a source at the focus sends out a beam that is parallel to the principal axis after reflection. Formally u = f gives 1/v = 1/f - 1/f = 0, so v is infinite.

The reflected rays from a convex mirror always diverge, so they can only appear to come from a point behind the mirror. That image is virtual and erect, and it always lies between the pole and the focus, so it is smaller than the object.

correct_answer: is complete but less bright than before
explanation: Light from each point of the object spreads over the whole aperture of the mirror. The uncovered upper half still receives rays from every point of the object and brings each set to its own image point, so the full image is formed. Only half as much light is now collected, so the image is dimmer.

correct_answer: slope is -1 and whose intercept on either axis has magnitude 1/f
explanation: Writing the mirror formula as 1/v = -(1/u) + 1/f shows a straight line of slope -1 with vertical intercept 1/f. By symmetry the intercept on the horizontal axis also has magnitude 1/f. Reading either intercept gives the focal length at once.

correct_answer: the object distance u is negative
explanation: Distances are measured from the pole and taken positive in the direction in which the incident light travels. A real object always lies on the side from which light comes, so u is always negative. A concave mirror has its focus in front of it, so f is negative, and a real image also forms in front, so v is negative.

correct_answer: real, inverted, of the same size and at the centre of curvature
explanation: Putting u = -R and f = -R/2 in 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives 1/v = -2/R + 1/R = -1/R, so v = -R. The image is real and also at the centre of curvature, and m = -v/u = -1, so it is inverted and of the same size.

For a spherical mirror of small aperture f = R / 2. With R = 30 cm the focal length is 30 / 2 = 15 cm. The negative sign in the Cartesian convention for a concave mirror concerns direction only; the magnitude is 15 cm.
sin C = 1/mu = 1/2, so C = 30°. Any ray inside the medium striking the boundary at more than 30° to the normal is totally internally reflected.

correct_answer: totally internally reflected at the hypotenuse and turned through 90°
explanation: Entering normally, the beam is undeviated and meets the hypotenuse at 45° to its normal. The critical angle is given by sin C = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C is about 41.8°. Since 45° is greater than 41.8°, total internal reflection occurs. A single reflection at a surface inclined at 45° to the beam turns it through 90°.

With air above, sin C = 1/(3/2) = 0.667 and C is about 42°. With water above, sin C = (4/3)/(3/2) = 8/9 = 0.889 and C is about 62.7°. Bringing the two refractive indices closer together makes it harder to trap the light, so a larger angle of incidence is now needed for total internal reflection.
From sin 30 = 1/mu we get 1/2 = 1/mu, so mu = 2. Then v = c/mu = (3 × 10⁸)/2 = 1.5 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

correct_answer: from a denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
explanation: Going from denser to rarer the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, and beyond it Snell law would require a sine greater than one, so no refracted ray exists and all the light is reflected back into the denser medium.

correct_answer: its critical angle is very small, so light entering it undergoes many total internal reflections before emerging
explanation: For diamond sin C = 1/2.42 = 0.413, so C is about 24°. Almost any ray inside the stone therefore meets a face at more than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected. The faces are cut so that the light finally leaves through the top, concentrating the brilliance where it is seen.

correct_answer: returns essentially the whole of the incident light energy
explanation: Above the critical angle Snell law admits no real refracted ray, so no energy is carried away into the rarer medium and the reflection is complete. A metal mirror always absorbs a few per cent at each reflection. This is why totally reflecting prisms are preferred to mirrors in periscopes and binoculars.

Here the denser medium is glass and the rarer is water, so sin C = mu_water / mu_glass = (4/3)/(3/2) = (4/3)(2/3) = 8/9 = 0.889. The critical angle is about 62.7°, larger than the 41.8° for glass and air, because water is closer in density to glass than air is.

correct_answer: air near the hot road is optically rarer, so light from the sky is totally internally reflected upwards
explanation: Air close to the hot road expands, becomes less dense and so has a smaller refractive index. A ray from the sky travelling downwards passes from denser upper layers into rarer lower layers, bending steadily away from the vertical until it meets a layer at more than the critical angle. It is then totally internally reflected and curves back up to the eye, which traces it back to a point on the road.

Since sin C = 1/mu, a larger refractive index gives a smaller sine and hence a smaller critical angle. Diamond has the largest index, 2.42, so sin C = 0.413 and C is about 24°, the smallest of the four. Water gives about 49°, crown glass about 42° and dense flint glass about 37°.

correct_answer: repeated total internal reflection at the boundary between the core and the cladding
explanation: The core has a slightly larger refractive index than the cladding, so rays that meet the boundary at more than the critical angle are totally internally reflected. Because total internal reflection returns all the energy, the light can bounce thousands of times with very little loss.

correct_answer: dark, being the second dark fringe
explanation: Path difference = (0.9 × 10⁻³ x 10⁻³) / 1 = 9 × 10⁻⁷ m. Dividing by λ = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m gives 1.5, so the path difference is 1.5 λ. This is an odd multiple of half a wavelength with n = 2, so the point is the second dark fringe.

correct_answer: equally spaced, the spacing being the same for all orders
explanation: Since the position of a bright fringe increases in direct proportion to the order n, the difference between consecutive positions is the constant λ x D / d. Hence the fringes are of equal width near the centre.
Extra optical path = (1.5 minus 1) × 6 × 10⁻⁶ = 3 × 10⁻⁶ m. Dividing by λ = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m gives 5, so the whole pattern shifts by 5 fringes towards the slit that carries the sheet.
Doubling D in beta = λ x D / d doubles the value of beta while λ and d stay fixed.
beta = (5 × 10⁻⁷ x 1) / 10⁻³ = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.5 mm. In a region of 1 cm = 10 mm, the number of bright fringes = 10 divided by 0.5 = 20.

correct_answer: white, because the path difference is zero for every wavelength there
explanation: The point equidistant from both slits has zero path difference. The condition for a maximum, path difference = n x λ with n = 0, is met by all the colours in white light at once, so their sum appears white.
The ratio of the new fringe width to the old one equals 4000 / 6000 = 2 / 3. The fringes therefore become closer together in the ratio 2 : 3.
The second bright fringe is at 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 mm and the second dark fringe is at (2 × 2 minus 1) × 0.6 / 2 = 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9 mm. The separation is 1.2 minus 0.9 = 0.3 mm, that is half a fringe width.
beta = 6 mm divided by 10 = 0.6 mm = 6 × 10⁻⁴ m. Then λ = beta x d / D = (6 × 10⁻⁴ x 10⁻³) / 1 = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m = 6000 Å.

correct_answer: the single slit diffraction pattern of the open slit, with no interference fringes
explanation: With only one slit open there is a single beam, so there is no path difference and no interference. What remains is the broad diffraction pattern produced by that one slit.

The condition n1 × 6000 = n2 × 4800 gives n1 / n2 = 4800 / 6000 = 4 / 5, so the smallest whole numbers are n1 = 4 for 6000 Å and n2 = 5 for 4800 Å. Then y = 4 × (6 × 10⁻⁷) × 1 / 10⁻³ = 2.4 × 10⁻³ m = 2.4 mm. The same value follows from 5 × (4.8 × 10⁻⁷) × 1 / 10⁻³.

correct_answer: come closer together, because the wavelength inside the liquid is smaller
explanation: Inside the liquid the wavelength becomes λ divided by mu, so the fringe width becomes beta divided by mu. Since mu is greater than one, the new fringe width is smaller and the fringes crowd together.
Setting the two directions equal gives n / m = d / a = 2, so n = 2m. Taking m = 1, 2, 3 gives the missing orders n = 2, 4, 6 and so on.

correct_answer: λ x D / d, where d is the slit separation and D is the slit to screen distance
explanation: The nth bright fringe lies at y = n x λ x D / d, so the gap between consecutive bright fringes is λ x D / d, which is the fringe width beta.

correct_answer: the third bright fringe of 4000 Å meets the second bright fringe of 6000 Å
explanation: The condition is n1 × 4000 = n2 × 6000, that is n1 / n2 = 6000 / 4000 = 3 / 2. The smallest whole numbers satisfying this are n1 = 3 and n2 = 2, so the third fringe of 4000 Å coincides with the second fringe of 6000 Å.
Replacing d by 2d in beta = λ x D / d gives a new fringe width λ x D / (2 x d), which is half the original value.

correct_answer: the electron waves scattered from successive atomic planes interfere constructively at that angle
explanation: The regularly spaced atomic planes scatter the incident electron waves. In directions where the path difference between waves from successive planes is a whole number of wavelengths the amplitudes add, producing a strong maximum. The angular position depends on the electron energy exactly as the de Broglie wavelength predicts.

√(54) = 7.35, so λ = 12.27 / 7.35 = 1.67 Å. The observed diffraction maximum at 50° corresponded to a wavelength of about 1.65 Å from the crystal spacing, in excellent agreement with the de Broglie prediction.

correct_answer: radiation and matter both show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others
explanation: Interference and diffraction of light require a wave description, while the photoelectric and Compton effects require photons. Similarly electrons show diffraction from crystals yet leave sharp tracks in a cloud chamber. Each experiment reveals one aspect; the two are complementary and never contradictory.

correct_answer: a smaller scattering angle, because the electron wavelength has become shorter
explanation: Increasing V shortens λ as 1 / √(V). For a fixed lattice spacing d, the constructive interference condition of the form d sin θ = n λ then gives a smaller sin θ, so the maximum moves to a smaller angle. This voltage dependence is itself strong evidence for the de Broglie relation.

correct_answer: the de Broglie wavelength of the accelerated electrons is far shorter than the wavelength of visible light
explanation: Visible light has a wavelength around 5000 Å, so an optical microscope cannot resolve detail much finer than that. Electrons accelerated through say 10000 V have λ = 12.27 / 100 = 0.1227 Å, thousands of times shorter, so the attainable resolution is enormously better.

Since λ is inversely proportional to √(V), we have V proportional to 1 / lambda². Reducing λ by a factor of 3 multiplies 1 / lambda² by 9, so V must be increased nine fold. For example 100 V giving 1.227 Å becomes 900 V giving 0.409 Å.

correct_answer: the wave nature of electrons predicted by de Broglie
explanation: Davisson and Germer scattered a beam of low energy electrons from a nickel single crystal and found a pronounced peak in the scattered intensity at a particular angle. This peak can only arise from constructive interference of waves, confirming that electrons possess a wavelength given by h / p.

correct_answer: the saturation photocurrent doubles while the stopping potential falls to zero
explanation: At 3100 Å the photon energy is 12400 / 3100 = 4.0 eV, so KE_max = 4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0 eV. At 6200 Å the photon energy is 12400 / 6200 = 2.0 eV, exactly the work function, so KE_max = 0 and the stopping potential falls to zero. Photon energy has halved at the same power, so the photon rate doubles. Under the stated assumption that each sufficiently energetic photon releases an electron and all released electrons are collected, the saturation current follows the photon rate and therefore doubles. Note that maximum kinetic energy and emission rate are separate quantities: frequency fixes the former, intensity fixes the latter.
At the point where the line meets the frequency axis KE_max is zero, so nu = nu_0 = 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Then W = h nu_0 = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ x 6 × 10¹⁴ = 3.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.475 eV.

A photon of energy h nu is absorbed by one electron. Part of this energy, W, is used in escaping from the surface, and the rest appears as kinetic energy. The most weakly bound electrons keep the largest share, so KE_max = h nu - W.

correct_answer: electrons are just barely liberated with essentially zero kinetic energy
explanation: Setting h nu = W in KE_max = h nu - W gives KE_max = 0. The most weakly bound electrons reach the surface with just enough energy to escape and emerge with vanishing speed, so the stopping potential is zero and the current is extremely small.

correct_answer: electrons from below the surface lose part of their energy before escaping
explanation: The work function is the minimum energy for escape and applies to the least tightly bound electrons at the surface. Electrons originating deeper must expend extra energy in collisions with the lattice, so they emerge with less than h nu - W. The observed spectrum therefore extends from zero up to KE_max.

First case KE_max = 4 - 2 = 2 eV. Second case KE_max = 6 - 2 = 4 eV. The ratio is 2 : 4 = 1 : 2. The ratio of kinetic energies is not the ratio of photon energies because of the constant work function.
Delta KE = h Delta nu = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ x 2 × 10¹⁴ = 1.32 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. In eV this is 1.32 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.825 eV. The work function cancels because it is unchanged.

correct_answer: does not appear at all, so KE_max is independent of intensity
explanation: The equation involves only the photon energy h nu and the metal's work function W. Intensity determines how many such photons arrive per second, and so fixes the current, but the energy transaction for each individual electron is unchanged.
From the first case W = 5 - 3 = 2 eV. For the second case KE_max = 7 - 2 = 5 eV. Note that the kinetic energy rose by 2 eV, exactly the rise in photon energy, since W is unchanged.

Light supplies energy to the loosely bound conduction electrons of the metal. If the energy exceeds the work function the electron escapes. The emitted particles carry negative charge and have the charge to mass ratio of the electron.

correct_answer: a measurable time lag should occur before emission when the light is very feeble, whereas emission is observed to be practically instantaneous
explanation: On the wave picture a very dim source would take hours to deliver the work function to a single electron spread over an atomic area. Experiment shows emission within about 10⁻⁹ s even for feeble light, because a single photon delivers its whole energy to one electron at once.

correct_answer: every electron emitted from the plate is then collected, so no further increase is possible
explanation: At small positive potential some slow electrons emitted sideways or backwards fail to reach the collector. As the potential rises, more of them are drawn in until all emitted electrons are collected. Then the current equals e times the number emitted per second and cannot rise further.

KE_max is fixed by the energy of a single photon minus the work function. Increasing intensity increases the number of photons per second, hence the current, but not the energy h nu carried by each photon. So KE_max stays the same.

Hertz observed in 1887 that a spark jumped more readily across a gap when the negative electrode was illuminated by ultraviolet light. Hallwachs and Lenard studied it in detail; Einstein explained it in 1905.

correct_answer: came from deeper inside the metal and lost energy in collisions before escaping
explanation: All electrons absorb the same energy h nu. The most weakly bound electrons at the surface need only the work function W to escape, so they emerge with KE_max = h nu - W. Electrons from deeper layers must do extra work and suffer collisions, so they emerge with less, giving a continuous spread from zero up to KE_max.

correct_answer: increase when the intensity of the incident light is increased
explanation: In the wave picture the electric field of the wave drives the electron; a larger amplitude, that is a larger intensity, would give the electron more energy. Experiment shows KE_max is completely independent of intensity and grows linearly with frequency, which is what Einstein's equation gives.

correct_answer: absorbs one whole photon and either escapes or gives the energy back to the lattice
explanation: The elementary photoelectric process is the absorption of one photon by one electron. The electron gains h nu at once. If h nu exceeds the work function W the electron can escape with kinetic energy up to h nu - W, otherwise the energy is shared with the lattice as heat.

correct_answer: the intensity of the incident light is doubled, the frequency being unchanged
explanation: Each absorbed photon can release at most one electron. Doubling the intensity at fixed frequency doubles the number of photons arriving per second, so the number of photoelectrons per second and the saturation current both double.

correct_answer: ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet light strongly while quartz transmits it
explanation: Metals such as zinc have a threshold in the ultraviolet. Ordinary soda glass cuts off wavelengths shorter than about 350 nm, so the light that could cause emission would never reach the plate. Quartz is transparent well into the ultraviolet.

correct_answer: the energy of the light is concentrated in localised quanta rather than spread over the wavefront
explanation: If light energy were spread uniformly over the wavefront, a dim beam would need minutes or hours to supply a few eV to one electron. Because energy arrives as photons of energy h nu, a single absorption event immediately supplies the whole energy, so emission is essentially instantaneous.

correct_answer: air molecules would scatter and absorb the emitted electrons before they reach the collector
explanation: Photoelectrons emitted with a few eV of kinetic energy would collide with gas molecules, lose energy and be deflected, so the measured current and stopping potential would not correspond to the emitted energies. Evacuation gives the electrons a free path.

correct_answer: Statement (i) is true and statement (ii) is false
explanation: Doubling the intensity at fixed frequency doubles the photon rate and hence the saturation current, so the first statement is correct. The energy given to each electron is h nu - W, which does not contain intensity, so the second statement is wrong.

correct_answer: decreases and becomes zero at a definite negative potential
explanation: As the collector is made negative, electrons must climb a potential barrier of energy e V. Electrons with lower kinetic energy are turned back, so the current falls. At V = V₀ even the fastest electrons are stopped and the current is zero.

correct_answer: The number of photoelectrons emitted per second
explanation: Intensity is the energy delivered per unit area per second, which at fixed frequency is proportional to the photon rate. More photons per second means more electrons per second. Energies per electron, and hence the stopping potential and the threshold, are untouched.
n = P / E = 20 / (4 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5 × 10¹⁹ photons per second. The very large number explains why the granular nature of light is not apparent in everyday experience.

correct_answer: undeviated, because the photon carries no electric charge
explanation: The photon is a chargeless quantum of the electromagnetic field. Since the electric force is q E and q = 0, no deflection occurs. This is one way to distinguish a beam of photons from a beam of electrons, which would be strongly deflected.
E = h nu = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ x 5 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ gives 2.06 eV, which lies in the visible region.
Power on the surface = 2 × 10⁻⁴ W. Energy per photon = 12400 / 5000 = 2.48 eV = 2.48 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. So n = 2 × 10⁻⁴ / 3.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ photons per second.
E = h nu = h c / λ and p = h / λ. Dividing, E / p = c, so E = p c. This is the massless limit of the relativistic relation E² = p² c² + m_0² c⁴.
Energy per photon = h c / λ = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ x 3 × 10⁸) / (6 × 10⁻⁷) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then n = P / E = 3.3 × 10⁻³ / 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1 × 10¹⁶ photons per second.

correct_answer: stays the same because the frequency does not change
explanation: On entering a medium the frequency is fixed by the source and does not change; the speed falls to c / n and the wavelength shortens to λ / n. Since E = h nu, the photon energy is unaltered. The momentum in the medium is h / (λ / n), which does change.

X rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength, so their photons carry the largest energy, typically thousands of eV. Visible photons carry a few eV. Radio photons, with wavelengths of metres, carry only about 10⁻⁶ eV.

Incoming momentum is +h / λ and outgoing is -h / λ, so the photon's momentum changes by 2h / λ. By conservation of momentum the surface receives 2h / λ. For an absorbing surface the transfer would be only h / λ, which is why a mirror feels twice the radiation pressure of a black surface.
E = 12400 / 6200 = 2 eV. Red light near 6200 Å therefore carries about 2 eV per photon, which is why only low work function metals such as caesium respond to it.

correct_answer: fewer photons per second, each of larger energy
explanation: Blue light has the higher frequency, so each blue photon carries more energy. Since the power P = n h nu is the same for both beams, n = P / (h nu) is smaller for the blue beam. Equal power means equal energy per second shared among fewer, more energetic packets.
Since p is inversely proportional to λ, p₁ / p₂ = lambda_2 / lambda_1 = 2 / 1. The shorter wavelength photon carries the larger momentum, and by E = p c also the larger energy.

correct_answer: zero, which is why it can travel with the speed of light
explanation: A photon always travels at c in vacuum. Relativistic mechanics allows this only for particles of zero rest mass. Its energy is E = h nu and its momentum p = E / c = h / λ, consistent with the relation E² = p² c² + m_0² c⁴ with m₀ = 0.
V₀ = KE_max / e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1 V. Whenever the maximum kinetic energy is expressed in eV, its numerical value equals the stopping potential in volt.
Putting nu = 0 in V₀ = (h / e) nu - W / e gives V₀ = -W / e. So the magnitude of the intercept on the potential axis multiplied by e gives the work function directly.

Let the photon energy at frequency nu be E, in eV. Then 1 = E - W and 3 = 2E - W. Subtracting the first from the second gives 2 = E, so E = 2 eV. Substituting back, W = E - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 eV. The threshold frequency is therefore half of nu.

The relation contains both nu and W. Raising the frequency raises V₀ at fixed metal; changing to a metal of larger work function lowers V₀ at fixed frequency. Only the intensity is absent from the relation.

h = e x slope = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 4.125 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Millikan measured this slope for several metals and found the same value each time, confirming Einstein's equation and giving an independent determination of h.

correct_answer: least negative potential of the collector at which the photocurrent becomes zero
explanation: As the collector is made more negative, electrons must overcome a retarding barrier. At V₀ even the fastest electron, of energy KE_max, is just turned back, so the current falls to zero. Hence e V₀ = KE_max.

correct_answer: 2.1 V negative with respect to the cathode
explanation: Photon energy = 12400 / 3100 = 4.0 eV. KE_max = 4.0 - 1.9 = 2.1 eV. The retarding voltage must therefore be at least 2.1 V with the collector negative; any smaller magnitude leaves the fastest electrons still able to cross.
Since lambda_0 W = h c is the same constant for both metals, lambda_1 / lambda_2 = W₂ / W₁ = 3 / 2. The metal with the smaller work function has the longer threshold wavelength.
lambda_0 = 300 nm = 3 × 10⁻⁷ m. nu_0 = c / lambda_0 = 3 × 10⁸ / 3 × 10⁻⁷ = 1 × 10¹⁵ Hz. The corresponding work function is 1240 / 300 = 4.13 eV.

Photon energy at 550 nm is 1240 / 550 = 2.25 eV. For emission the work function must not exceed this, so a low work function material such as caesium coated antimony is used. Platinum with 5.65 eV would be useless in the visible region.
For M, KE_max = 6 - 2 = 4 eV. For N, KE_max = 6 - 4 = 2 eV. Since v_max is proportional to √(KE_max), the ratio of speeds is √(4) : √(2) = 2 : √(2) = √(2) : 1, that is about 1.41 : 1.

correct_answer: caesium, sodium and potassium all fail while Z emits
explanation: Compare 1.8 eV with each work function. It is smaller than 2.14 eV, 2.75 eV and 2.30 eV, so caesium, sodium and potassium give no emission. It exceeds 1.5 eV, so metal Z emits with KE_max = 0.3 eV.

correct_answer: minimum energy required to just free an electron from the metal surface
explanation: The work function W is the least energy that must be supplied to a conduction electron at the Fermi level for it to escape from the surface with zero kinetic energy. It is characteristic of the metal and its surface condition and is usually a few eV.

Emission needs h nu greater than W. Here h nu = 3.0 eV, which exceeds 2.14 eV for caesium and 2.75 eV for sodium but falls well short of 5.65 eV for platinum. So caesium and sodium emit; platinum does not.
Planck constant has dimensions of energy times time, and frequency has dimensions of inverse time, so h nu_0 has the dimensions of energy, M L² T⁻². It is measured in joule or in electron volt.

correct_answer: its de Broglie wavelength, about 2 × 10⁻³⁴ m, is far too small to be detected by any means
explanation: λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 20) = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 3 = 2.2 × 10⁻³⁴ m. No aperture or grating of that spacing exists, so diffraction effects can never be exhibited. The wave nature becomes apparent only for very light particles such as electrons.

correct_answer: every particle that is in motion, whether charged or neutral
explanation: The de Broglie relation involves only Planck constant and the momentum. Charge does not appear, so neutrons, atoms and even molecules show wave behaviour. Since p must be non zero for a finite wavelength, the particle must be in motion.
λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, that is 2 Å. This is of the order of interatomic spacings, so such electrons can be diffracted by crystals.

correct_answer: are neither mechanical nor electromagnetic in nature
explanation: A matter wave requires no medium, so it is not mechanical, and it is associated with neutral particles such as neutrons as well as charged ones, so it is not electromagnetic. Its amplitude relates to the probability of finding the particle, and the wavelength is h / p.
From K = (1/2) m v² = p² / (2 m) we get p = √(2 m K). Substituting into λ = h / p gives λ = h / √(2 m K). Both larger mass and larger kinetic energy shorten the wavelength.
Momentum p = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ x 2.2 × 10⁶ = 2.0 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. Then λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 2.0 × 10⁻²⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, which is 3.3 Å.

correct_answer: the same momentum but different energies
explanation: Both satisfy p = h / λ, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. The photon energy is p c while the electron kinetic energy is p² / (2 m) = p c x (p / (2 m c)). Since p is far smaller than m c for slow electrons, the electron energy is far less than the photon energy.
de Broglie extended the photon relation p = h / λ to material particles, proposing λ = h / p. For a particle of mass m and speed v this is λ = h / (m v). Larger momentum means shorter wavelength.

Since λ is inversely proportional to v at fixed mass, doubling v halves λ. Note that the kinetic energy in this case becomes four times as large, consistent with λ being inversely proportional to √(K).

With K the same for both, lambda_alpha / lambda_proton = √(m_proton / m_alpha) = √(1 / 4) = 1 / 2. So the alpha particle wave is half as long as the proton wave. At the same kinetic energy a heavier particle always has the shorter wavelength.

correct_answer: much shorter, because the proton has much larger momentum
explanation: At the same speed, lambda_proton / lambda_electron = m_electron / m_proton, about 1 / 1836. The proton wave is therefore about 1836 times shorter. A heavier particle at the same speed always has the shorter de Broglie wavelength.
The electron gains kinetic energy e V, so p = √(2 m e V) and λ = h / √(2 m e V). Substituting h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives λ = 12.27 / √(V) angstrom.

Eliminating the speed between the force balance and the quantisation condition gives r₁ proportional to 1/m for a fixed charge and fixed quantisation rule. Replacing the electron by a particle 207 times heavier therefore shrinks the first orbit by the same factor. Numerically r = 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m divided by 207, which is 2.56 × 10⁻¹³ m, so about 2.6 × 10⁻¹³ m. This is why the muon spends much of its time close to the nucleus and is sensitive to the nuclear size.

The electron passes a given point once per revolution, so the equivalent current is I = e/T = e v/(2 π r). Substituting v proportional to 1/n and r proportional to n squared gives I proportional to (1/n)/(n²) = 1/n³. The current therefore falls off very rapidly for the outer orbits.

The Bohr condition gives L = n h/(2 π). For the third orbit n = 3, so L = 3h/(2 π), which may also be written as 1.5 h/π. Angular momentum increases in equal steps of h/(2 π) from one orbit to the next.

The period of a circular orbit is T = 2 π r/v. Substituting r proportional to n² and v proportional to 1/n gives T proportional to n² divided by 1/n, that is T proportional to n³. The electron therefore takes twenty seven times as long to complete an orbit at n = 3 as at n = 1.
For n = 3, E₃ = -13.6/9 eV. Carrying out the division, 13.6/9 = 1.511, so E₃ = -1.51 eV. The levels crowd together as n increases, approaching zero for a free electron.

Combining the quantisation condition m v r = n h/(2 π) with the radius result r proportional to n squared gives v proportional to n/r, that is v proportional to n/n² = 1/n. The electron therefore moves more slowly in the outer orbits. For hydrogen the speed in the first orbit is about 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

A singly ionised helium ion has one electron and Z = 2. For n = 2 the radius is r = 0.53 × 4/2 = 1.06 Å, which is twice the hydrogen ground state radius. The energy is E = -13.6 × 4/4 = -13.6 eV, which happens to equal the hydrogen ground state energy. The stronger nuclear charge pulls the orbit in and deepens the binding.

The requirement is 0.53 × 2²/Z = 0.53, that is 4/Z = 1, so Z = 4. A triply ionised beryllium ion in its state n = 2 therefore has the same orbital radius as hydrogen in its ground state, although its energy, -13.6 × 16/4 = -54.4 eV, is four times deeper.

Dividing, 2.12/0.53 = 4, and since this equals n squared, n = 2. The angular momentum is then L = 2h/(2 π) = h/π. Note that the radius grows as the square of n while the angular momentum grows only as the first power of n.
Since the period varies as n cubed, the frequency of revolution varies as 1/n cubed. Going from n = 1 to n = 2 divides the frequency by 2 cubed, that is by 8, giving f/8.

Writing the Coulomb force as the centripetal force, m v²/r = k e²/r², and eliminating v using L = m v r, one obtains r = L²/(m k e²). The total energy is E = -k e²/(2r) = -m k² e⁴/(2 L²), so the magnitude of the binding energy varies as 1/L². Halving the quantised angular momentum therefore multiplies the binding energy by four, giving E₁ = 4 × (-13.6) = -54.4 eV. The corresponding radius would shrink to one quarter, that is 0.1325 Å.

The magnetic moment of a current loop is the current times the enclosed area, so mu = (e v/(2 π r)) x π r², which simplifies to e v r/2. Since v is proportional to 1/n and r is proportional to n squared, the product v r is proportional to n. Hence mu is proportional to n. Equivalently mu = (e/2m) L, and L itself is proportional to n.

Since the orbital speed varies as 1/n, moving from n = 1 to n = 3 divides the speed by 3, giving v/3. Numerically, if v = 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in the first orbit, the speed in the third orbit is about 7.3 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
Dividing the given radius by the first Bohr radius, 4.77/0.53 = 9. Since this ratio equals n squared, n = 3. A quick check confirms that 0.53 × 9 = 4.77 Å.

For a one electron ion the energy scales as the square of the nuclear charge. With Z = 3 and n = 1, E₁ = -13.6 × 9 = -122.4 eV. The electron is bound nine times more tightly than in hydrogen, so the ionisation energy of this ion is 122.4 eV.
Since r_n = 0.53 n² angstrom, the ratio r₃/r₁ equals 9/1. In absolute terms r₃ = 0.53 × 9 = 4.77 Å while r₁ = 0.53 Å.

correct_answer: n h/(2 π), where n is a positive integer
explanation: Bohr postulated that an electron can occupy only those circular orbits in which its angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/(2 π). Writing L = m v r, the condition is m v r = n h/(2 π) with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. The integer n is the principal quantum number and it labels the stationary orbit.
The ground state is n = 1, so the first excited state is n = 2. Then E₂ = -13.6/4 = -3.4 eV. The atom is less tightly bound in this state, which is why the energy is closer to zero.

Balancing the Coulomb attraction against the centripetal requirement, m v²/r = k e²/r², gives m v² = k e²/r and hence KE = k e²/(2r). The electrostatic potential energy of the electron and proton is PE = -k e²/r. Dividing, KE/PE = -1/2, independent of the orbit. This is the virial result for an inverse square attraction.

The ground state is the lowest energy state, for which n = 1. Substituting gives E₁ = -13.6/1 = -13.6 eV. The energy is negative because the electron is bound to the proton; energy must be supplied to free it.

For a circular orbit under the inverse square Coulomb attraction the electrostatic force supplies the centripetal force, which leads to KE = k e²/(2r) and PE = -k e²/r. Hence PE = -2 KE and the total energy E = KE + PE = -KE. With E = -3.4 eV the kinetic energy is +3.4 eV and the potential energy is 2 × (-3.4) = -6.8 eV. Adding them returns -3.4 eV, as required.

The Bohr radius grows as the square of the principal quantum number, r_n = 0.53 n² angstrom. For n = 2 this gives r = 0.53 × 4 = 2.12 Å. The second orbit is therefore four times as far from the nucleus as the first.

correct_answer: contains a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths of the electron
explanation: De Broglie proposed that the electron in an orbit behaves as a wave that must close on itself, so the circumference must be an integral number of wavelengths, 2 π r = n λ. Substituting λ = h/(m v) gives 2 π r = n h/(m v), which rearranges to m v r = n h/(2 π). This is exactly Bohr's quantisation postulate, now given a physical basis.

correct_answer: does not radiate energy even though it is accelerated
explanation: Bohr simply asserted, in contradiction to classical electromagnetism, that an electron in one of the allowed orbits is in a stationary state and does not radiate. Radiation occurs only when the electron makes a transition from one stationary state to another. This postulate removes the collapse predicted by classical theory and permits stable atoms.
Bohr quantization gives mvr = nℏ = nh/(2π).

An electron accelerated through 10.2 V arrives with 10.2 eV of kinetic energy, exactly the amount needed to lift a ground state hydrogen atom to n = 2. Hence the first excitation potential is 10.2 V. In the Franck and Hertz type experiment this shows up as the first dip in the transmitted electron current.

Ionisation means raising the electron from its bound level to the free state of zero energy. From the ground state at -13.6 eV, the energy required is 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6 eV. Any photon of higher energy will also ionise the atom, the surplus appearing as kinetic energy of the freed electron.

The ionisation potential is the accelerating potential difference through which an electron must fall to acquire just enough energy to ionise the atom. Since an electron accelerated through V volt gains V electron volt of energy, an ionisation energy of 13.6 eV corresponds to an ionisation potential of 13.6 V. The number is the same but the unit is the volt, not the electron volt.

After absorbing the photon the energy of the atom is -13.6 + 12.09 = -1.51 eV. Setting -13.6/n² = -1.51 gives n² = 9, so n = 3. Note that the photon energy matches this gap exactly, which is precisely why absorption is possible.

correct_answer: the collision is elastic and the electron retains practically all of its kinetic energy
explanation: The lowest amount of energy a ground state hydrogen atom can accept is 10.2 eV, the gap to the level n = 2. A projectile electron carrying only 10 eV has less than this, so no internal transition is possible. The collision is therefore elastic, and because the atom is about eighteen hundred times heavier than the electron, the electron rebounds with essentially unchanged kinetic energy.

The atom needs at least 3.4 eV to reach the free state of zero energy. The longest wavelength corresponds to exactly this threshold energy, so λ = 12400/3.4 = 3647 Å. Photons of shorter wavelength carry more energy and also ionise, the excess appearing as kinetic energy of the released electron.

The energy of the level n = 3 is -13.6/9 = -1.51 eV, so 1.51 eV lifts the electron to the free state of zero energy. The higher the initial level, the smaller this binding energy becomes, tending to zero for very large n.

For this ion E₁ = -54.4 eV and E₂ = -54.4/4 = -13.6 eV. The first excitation energy is therefore -13.6 - (-54.4) = 40.8 eV. This is four times the corresponding hydrogen value, as expected from the Z squared scaling of the level energies.

correct_answer: passes through essentially unabsorbed because 11.0 eV matches no energy gap from the ground state
explanation: From the ground state the permitted absorption energies are 10.2 eV to reach n = 2, 12.09 eV to reach n = 3, 12.75 eV to reach n = 4 and so on up to 13.6 eV for ionisation. The value 11.0 eV lies between two of these and matches none of them, and it is below the ionisation threshold, so no free electron state is available either. The photon is therefore not absorbed and the gas is transparent at this energy. This is unlike a collision with an electron, where the surplus energy can be carried away as kinetic energy.

The first excited state is n = 2, whose energy is -3.4 eV. Starting from the ground state at -13.6 eV, the energy that must be supplied is -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV. This is the first excitation energy.

The second excited state is n = 3, whose energy is -13.6/9 = -1.51 eV. Starting from the ground state at -13.6 eV, the energy needed is -1.51 - (-13.6) = 12.09 eV. So the second excitation potential of hydrogen is 12.09 V.

Ionising from n = 2 means raising the atom from -3.4 eV to zero energy, so 3.4 eV suffices. An excited atom is easier to ionise than a ground state atom, which is why ionisation energy always refers to the ground state unless another state is named.

The energies needed from the ground state are 10.2 eV for n = 2, 12.09 eV for n = 3 and 12.75 eV for n = 4. A 12.5 eV electron can supply the 12.09 eV needed for n = 3, keeping the remaining 0.41 eV as kinetic energy, but it cannot supply the 12.75 eV needed for n = 4. So the highest populated level is n = 3, and the number of distinct downward transitions is 3 × 2/2 = 3, namely from 3 to 2, from 3 to 1 and from 2 to 1.

A singly ionised helium ion has a single electron moving around a nucleus of charge 2e, so Z = 2. Its ground state energy is -13.6 × 4 = -54.4 eV and the energy needed to free the electron is 54.4 eV. This is why the second ionisation energy of helium is much larger than the first.

The longest wavelength member of the Lyman series has photon energy 13.6 × (1 - 1/4) = 10.2 eV and the shortest has 13.6 eV. Since wavelength varies inversely with energy, the ratio of wavelengths is 13.6 : 10.2, which simplifies to 4 : 3. The same result follows from the Rydberg formula as (1/(3/4)) divided by (1/1).
The photon energy is 13.6 (1/4 - 1/9) = 13.6 × (9 - 4)/36 = 13.6 × 5/36 = 1.889 eV. The wavelength follows as 12400/1.889 = 6564 Å, so about 6563 Å. This is the familiar red line of hydrogen.

For the Balmer series n₁ = 2, so the limiting photon energy is 13.6/4 = 3.4 eV. Then λ = 12400/3.4 = 3647 Å. This lies just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, which is why the Balmer series is only partly visible.
After absorption the energy of the atom is -13.6 + 12.75 = -0.85 eV. Setting -13.6/n² = -0.85 gives n² = 16, so n = 4. From the level n = 4 the number of distinct downward transitions is 4 × 3/2 = 6.
For the Balmer series n₁ = 2, so λ = 4/R = 4/(1.1 × 10⁷) m. Carrying out the division gives 3.64 × 10⁻⁷ m, that is 364 nm. This agrees with the value 3647 Å obtained from the energy of 3.4 eV.

The photon energy is E₂ - E₁ in magnitude, that is 13.6 (1/n_1² - 1/n_2²) eV with n₁ the lower level. Dividing by h c converts this into a wave number, giving 1/λ = R (1/n_1² - 1/n_2²) where R is the Rydberg constant, about 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. Because n₂ is larger than n₁ the bracket is positive, as it must be for emission.

Working out the photon energies, the transition from n = 3 to n = 2 gives 1.89 eV, from n = 2 to n = 1 gives 10.2 eV, from n = 4 to n = 3 gives 1.51 - 0.85 = 0.66 eV and from n = 5 to n = 4 gives 0.85 - 0.54 = 0.31 eV. Only 1.89 eV falls inside the visible band, and the corresponding wavelength of 6563 Å is the red hydrogen line.

Each distinct pair of levels among n = 1, 2, 3 and 4 gives one spectral line. The number of such pairs is 4 × 3/2 = 6. Listing them, the transitions are from 4 to 3, 4 to 2, 4 to 1, 3 to 2, 3 to 1 and 2 to 1. Three of these belong to the Lyman series, two to the Balmer series and one to the Paschen series.

Setting the upper level to infinity, the shortest wavelength of a series is λ = n_1²/R. For the Lyman series n₁ = 1, giving 1/R, and for the Balmer series n₁ = 2, giving 4/R. The ratio is therefore 1 : 4. Numerically this is 912 Å against 3647 Å, which indeed differ by a factor of four.

correct_answer: from a very high level to n = 1
explanation: The photon energy is the difference between the two level energies. The greatest possible difference is obtained by falling from the top of the ladder, where the energy is essentially zero, to the deepest level, n = 1, at -13.6 eV. That gives 13.6 eV and a wavelength of 912 Å. Every other listed transition releases less energy and so gives a longer wavelength.

The series limit photon carries the full ionisation energy of the ground state, 13.6 eV. Using λ = 12400/13.6 Å gives 911.8 Å, so about 912 Å. Every other Lyman line has a smaller photon energy and hence a longer wavelength.

As the upper level rises, the term 1/n_2² tends to zero and the photon energy approaches its greatest value. For the Lyman series this limiting energy is 13.6 eV, produced when a free electron with negligible kinetic energy is captured into the ground state. The corresponding wavelength, 912 Å, is the shortest in the series.

The first Balmer line comes from n = 3 to n = 2, so the second comes from n = 4 to n = 2. Its photon energy is 13.6 (1/4 - 1/16) = 13.6 × 3/16 = 2.55 eV. The wavelength is 12400/2.55 = 4863 Å, which is blue green light.

In the Balmer series the electron drops from any level with n greater than 2 down to n = 2. The first line, from n = 3 to n = 2, has a photon energy of 1.89 eV and a wavelength of about 6563 Å, which is red light. Four Balmer lines fall in the visible region, which is why this series was discovered first.

Every Lyman line corresponds to an electron falling to n = 1, so the smallest photon energy in the series is 13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2 eV and the largest is 13.6 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, these correspond to wavelengths of 1216 Å and 912 Å, both well short of the violet limit of about 4000 Å. The whole series therefore lies in the ultraviolet.
Substituting the quantum numbers, 1/λ = R (1/1 - 1/4) = 3R/4. Taking the reciprocal gives λ = 4/(3R). With R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ this evaluates to 1.216 × 10⁻⁷ m, in agreement with the value 1216 Å.

The smallest photon energy in the Lyman series comes from the closest pair of levels, n = 2 down to n = 1. That energy is 13.6 (1/1 - 1/4) = 13.6 × 0.75 = 10.2 eV. The wavelength is 12400/10.2 = 1215.7 Å, so about 1216 Å.

The levels are E₁ = -13.6 eV, E₂ = -3.40 eV, E₃ = -1.51 eV and E₄ = -0.85 eV. The difference between the level at -0.85 eV and the level at -3.40 eV is 2.55 eV, which matches the emitted photon exactly. So the electron has fallen from n = 4 to n = 2, giving the second line of the Balmer series at 4863 Å.

In hydrogen the transition from n = 2 to n = 1 releases 13.6 (1 - 1/4) = 10.2 eV. For the helium ion Z = 2, so the level energies are E_n = -54.4/n² eV, giving E₁ = -54.4, E₂ = -13.6, E₃ = -6.04 and E₄ = -3.4 eV. The difference between the level at -3.4 eV and the level at -13.6 eV is 10.2 eV, matching the hydrogen line exactly. In general, multiplying every quantum number by Z reproduces the hydrogen spectrum.

The most energetic Paschen photon is the series limit, of energy 13.6/9 = 1.51 eV, and its wavelength is 12400/1.51 = 8200 Å. Since visible light stops at about 7500 Å, every Paschen line is longer in wavelength than visible red light and so lies in the infrared.
The Balmer series consists of transitions from higher levels to n = 2 and lies mainly in the visible region.

First the energy in MeV is 0.02 × 931.5 = 18.63 MeV. Expressed in electron volt this is 1.863 × 10⁷ eV. Multiplying by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per eV gives 2.98 × 10⁻¹² J, so about 3.0 × 10⁻¹² J. For comparison, a chemical reaction between two atoms releases only a few times 10⁻¹⁹ J, which is why nuclear processes are millions of times more energetic.
Dividing, 128/16 = 8 MeV per nucleon. This value sits close to the flat top of the binding energy curve, so a nuclide of this kind is comparatively tightly bound.

The helium nucleus contains four nucleons, so the binding energy per nucleon is 28/4 = 7 MeV. This is unusually high for such a light nucleus, which is why the helium nucleus is emitted as a unit in alpha decay.

The constituent mass is 2 × 1.00728 + 2 × 1.00867 = 2.01456 + 2.01734 = 4.03190 u. Subtracting the actual nuclear mass, delta m = 4.03190 - 4.00151 = 0.03039 u. Multiplying by 931.5 gives 28.31 MeV. Dividing by four nucleons gives about 7.08 MeV per nucleon.

correct_answer: short ranged, so that each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours
explanation: If every nucleon attracted every other nucleon, the total binding energy would grow roughly as the square of the mass number and the binding energy per nucleon would rise steadily with A. In fact the nuclear force acts only over about one femtometre, so a nucleon deep inside a nucleus is bound to a fixed small number of neighbours no matter how large the nucleus is. The total binding energy therefore grows in proportion to A and the binding energy per nucleon stays nearly constant, which is the property called saturation.

The total binding energy of a heavy nucleus is large simply because it contains many nucleons. To compare nuclei of different sizes one must ask how tightly each individual nucleon is held, which is the binding energy divided by the mass number. Iron group nuclei, with about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, are the most stable on this measure even though uranium has a far larger total binding energy.

The mass defect is stated to be 0.00240 u. Multiplying, 0.00240 × 931.5 = 2.2356 MeV, so about 2.24 MeV. Dividing by the two nucleons gives a binding energy per nucleon of only about 1.1 MeV, which is why the deuteron is a very loosely bound nucleus.

Dividing, 931.5/931.5 = 1, so the mass defect is exactly 1 u, which is 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. A nucleus whose constituents lose a whole atomic mass unit on assembly is a moderately heavy one; for comparison, the helium nucleus loses only about 0.03 u.

Comparing the four values, 8.8 MeV per nucleon is the largest, so the nuclide Q is held together most tightly per nucleon and is the most stable. The value 8.8 MeV corresponds to the peak of the binding energy curve near mass number 56, while 1.1 MeV per nucleon is characteristic of the very loosely bound deuteron.

The parent has a total binding energy of 240 × 7.6 = 1824 MeV. The two fragments together have 240 × 8.5 = 2040 MeV. The difference, 2040 - 1824 = 216 MeV, is released. Equivalently the gain of 0.9 MeV per nucleon is multiplied by the 240 nucleons involved.

Binding energy is the energy that was given up when nucleons assembled. If the products are more tightly bound than the reactants, the extra binding energy appears as kinetic energy of the products and as radiation. Equivalently, the total rest mass falls and the lost mass appears as energy. Both fission of very heavy nuclei and fusion of very light ones move the system towards the peak of the binding energy curve, so both release energy.

Removing a neutron leaves a nuclide of the same element with one fewer nucleon. Since a free neutron has zero binding energy, the energy that must be supplied equals the loss of binding energy, that is 128 - 112 = 16 MeV. Note that this is twice the average binding energy per nucleon of 8 MeV, which shows that the separation energy of a particular nucleon can differ considerably from the average value.

The helium nucleus has a total binding energy of 4 × 7.0 = 28.0 MeV. Each deuteron has 2 × 1.1 = 2.2 MeV, so the two together have 4.4 MeV. The energy released is 28.0 - 4.4 = 23.6 MeV. The reaction releases energy because the product lies much higher on the binding energy curve than the reactants.

Multiplying 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg by the square of 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ gives 1.49 × 10⁻¹⁰ J. Dividing by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per eV gives 9.315 × 10⁸ eV, that is 931.5 MeV. This conversion turns any mass defect expressed in atomic mass units straight into a binding energy in MeV.

Multiplying, 0.5 × 931.5 = 465.75 MeV. This is the energy that would have to be supplied to pull the nucleus apart into its separate free nucleons, and equally the energy that was released when they came together.

correct_answer: the amount by which the sum of the masses of its free nucleons exceeds the mass of the nucleus
explanation: When free nucleons combine to form a nucleus, energy is released, and by the mass energy relation the assembled nucleus is lighter than its separated constituents. The missing mass is the mass defect. For a stable nucleus it is always positive, and multiplying it by c squared gives the binding energy.

Isobars contain the same total number of nucleons but distribute them differently between protons and neutrons, so they are different chemical elements. The nuclide with Z = 18 and A = 40 and the nuclide with Z = 20 and A = 40 form a familiar pair. Since the mass number is the same, isobars have very nearly equal masses and, by the relation R = R₀ A¹⁄³, equal nuclear radii.

Dividing, 2.3 × 10¹⁷ divided by 1.0 × 10³ gives 2.3 × 10¹⁴. So a spoonful of nuclear matter would weigh as much as a mountain of ordinary matter. The huge factor reflects the fact that atoms are almost entirely empty, with the mass confined to a volume about 10⁻¹⁵ of the atomic volume.

Experiments show that the volume of a nucleus is proportional to the number of nucleons it contains. Since volume is proportional to the cube of the radius, R³ is proportional to A and hence R is proportional to A¹⁄³. Writing the constant of proportionality as R₀ gives R = R₀ A¹⁄³ with R₀ about 1.2 fm.
Dividing, R/R₀ = 4.8/1.2 = 4. Cubing this gives A = 4³ = 64. As a check, the cube root of 64 is 4 and 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 fm, which is the given radius.

The mass number varies as the cube of the radius, so A₂ = 64 × (1.25)³. Now (1.25)³ = 1.953125, and 64 × 1.953125 = 125. So a nuclide of mass number 125 has a radius 1.25 times that of a nuclide of mass number 64, since the cube roots are 5 and 4 respectively.

correct_answer: the same atomic number but different mass numbers
explanation: The atomic number Z fixes the chemical element, so isotopes are different forms of the same element. They contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. Hydrogen with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3 is the standard example. Isotopes have almost identical chemical behaviour because chemistry depends on the electron count, which equals Z.

correct_answer: stays practically the same for all nuclei
explanation: The mass of a nucleus is about A times the nucleon mass m, while its volume is (4/3) π R³ = (4/3) π R_0³ A. Dividing, the mass number cancels and the density becomes 3m/(4 π R_0³), a constant of about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Nuclear matter therefore has the same density in a light nucleus as in a heavy one, which is why nuclear matter is often described as incompressible.

The cube root of 8 is 2 and the cube root of 216 is 6, so the radii are in the ratio 2 : 6, that is 1 : 3. For the density, the mass is proportional to A and the volume is also proportional to A, so the two dependences cancel exactly and every nucleus has the same density. The density ratio is therefore 1 : 1. This constancy is the physical content behind the empirical radius relation.

Since R = R₀ A¹⁄³, the volume (4/3) π R³ equals (4/3) π R_0³ A, which is directly proportional to the mass number. Hence the volumes are in the ratio 16 : 128, that is 1 : 8. The radii themselves are in the ratio 1 : 2, being the cube roots of 16 and 128.

The neutron number is N = A - Z. Isotones have equal N but different Z and different A. The nuclide with Z = 6 and A = 14 has eight neutrons, and so does the nuclide with Z = 8 and A = 16, so these two are isotones.
For the nuclide P the neutron number is 14 - 6 = 8. For the nuclide Q it is 16 - 8 = 8. The neutron numbers agree while both the atomic numbers and the mass numbers differ, so the pair are isotones.

The mass number cancels, leaving ρ = m divided by (4/3) π R_0³. First R_0³ = (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³ = 1.728 × 10⁻⁴⁵ m³. Multiplying by 4 π/3 = 4.19 gives a volume per nucleon of 7.24 × 10⁻⁴⁵ m³. Dividing the nucleon mass by this, ρ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷/7.24 × 10⁻⁴⁵ = 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

Taking cube roots, the cube root of 27 is 3 and the cube root of 125 is 5. Hence the radii are in the ratio 3 : 5. The mass numbers differ by a factor of about 4.6 while the radii differ by less than a factor of 2, which shows how slowly nuclear size grows with mass.

The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, so the neutron number is N = A - Z = 238 - 92 = 146. Heavy nuclei carry many more neutrons than protons because the extra neutrons help to offset the mutual electrostatic repulsion of the protons.

Inverting the radius relation gives A = (R/R₀)³, so the mass number varies as the cube of the radius. Doubling the radius therefore multiplies the mass number by 2 cubed, that is by 8. Equivalently the nuclear volume, and hence the number of nucleons, has increased eightfold.
The cube root of 27 is 3, so R = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ x 3 = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, that is 3.6 fm. This is roughly one hundred thousand times smaller than the radius of the corresponding atom.

correct_answer: Both statements are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
explanation: A rise in binding energy per nucleon corresponds to a decrease in total mass, and the mass difference is released as energy.

correct_answer: The total rest mass of products is smaller than that of reactants
explanation: For released energy Q, the mass decrease is Δm = Q/c²; charge and nucleon number remain conserved.
Nuclear radius R = R₀A¹⁄³; multiplying A by 8 multiplies R by 2.

correct_answer: Both fusion of light nuclei and fission of very heavy nuclei
explanation: Both processes move products toward higher binding energy per nucleon, reducing total mass and releasing energy.

At θ = 60°, sin(θ/2) = sin 30° = 1/2, so (sin(θ/2))⁴ = 1/16 and N is proportional to 16. At θ = 120°, sin(θ/2) = sin 60° = 0.866, so (sin(θ/2))⁴ = (0.75)² = 0.5625 and N is proportional to 1/0.5625 = 1.78. The required ratio is 16 divided by 1.78, which is 9. So nine times as many alpha particles appear at 60° as at 120°.

correct_answer: the positive charge and almost the whole mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small volume
explanation: To turn an energetic alpha particle through more than 90° the repulsive Coulomb force must be enormous, which is possible only if the alpha particle can approach very close to a large positive charge. In a uniformly spread positive charge the field inside falls towards zero at the centre and no such force arises. The rare violent deflections therefore require the positive charge to be compressed into a tiny volume, and since the alpha particle is scarcely able to move that centre, essentially all the atomic mass must sit there too.

For the proton, d = (1/(4 π ε₀)) (1)(Z) e² / K. For the alpha particle the projectile charge is doubled and the kinetic energy is four times larger, so its closest approach is (1/(4 π ε₀)) (2)(Z) e² / (4K), which equals one half of the proton value. Hence the alpha particle stops at d/2.

correct_answer: radiate continuously, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in a very short time
explanation: In the Rutherford picture the electron moves in a circle, so it has a centripetal acceleration. Classical electrodynamics requires an accelerated charge to emit electromagnetic radiation, so the electron would steadily lose energy, its orbital radius would shrink and it would fall into the nucleus in a time of the order of 10⁻⁸ s. The model therefore predicts that no atom can be stable. It also predicts a continuously changing frequency of emitted radiation, that is a continuous spectrum, whereas atoms in fact emit sharp lines.

correct_answer: smallest, tending to zero for a head on collision
